title: Splunkdbconnectmailmarshalintegrationdatabasequeriesusingpowershell
summary: Imported personal-notes SPL query from the "Splunkdbconnectmailmarshalintegrationdatabasequeriesusingpowershell" topic.
purpose: Originally captured in a personal Splunk notes wiki under the topic "Splunkdbconnectmailmarshalintegrationdatabasequeriesusingpowershell". Not independently re-authored — review before relying on it.
spl:
$connection = new-object System.Data.SqlClient.SqlConnection
$datasource = " SQL SERVER "
$database = "MailMarshal"
$connectionstring = "Server=$datasource;Database=$database;Integrated Security=SSPI;"
$connection.connectionstring=$connectionstring
$connection.open()
$query = @"
SELECT [Message].[TimeLogged]
      ,[Message].[BlockNumber]
      ,[Message].[BlockRecipientIndex]
      ,[Message].[MessageName]
      ,[Message].[ServerId]
      ,[Message].[MessageSize]
      ,[Message].[Subject]
      ,[Message].[TimeArrived]
      ,[Message].[FromUser]
      ,[Message].[FromDomain]
      ,[Message].[FromLocal]
      ,[Message].[Edition]
      ,[Message].[ActionType]
      ,[Message].[Classification]
      ,[Message].[Description]
      ,[Message].[RecipientUser]
      ,[Message].[RecipientDomain]
      ,[Message].[RecipientLocal]
      ,[Message].[FolderID]
      ,[Message].[Deleted]
      ,[Message].[SessionNumber]
      ,[Message].[BytesSent]
      ,[Message].[FirstInBlock]
      ,[Message].[ParentEdition]
      ,[Message].[HasAttachments]
	  ,[Content].[AttachmentId]
	  ,[Content].[ParentAttachmentId]
	  ,[Content].[FileType]
	  ,[Content].[FileName]
	  ,[Content].[FileSize]
      ,[Message].[IsTerminal]
      ,[Message].[MessageBody]
      ,[Message].[SpamCensorType]
      ,[Message].[RuleName]
  FROM [MailMarshal].[dbo].[Message]
	  ,[MailMarshal].[dbo].[Content]
WHERE [Content].[MessageName] = [Message].[MessageName]
"@
$command=$connection.createCommand()
$command.commandtext=$query
$result = $command.ExecuteReader()
$table = new-object "System.Data.Datatable"
$table.Load($result)
$output=$table|select filetype,fromdomain |sort-object -property fromdomain|group-object filetype,fromdomain
$output|foreach{
    $properties = @{
        'FromDomain' = ($_.name -split ", ")[1]
        'FileType' = ($_.name -split ", ")[0]
        'Count' = $_.count
    }
    $psobject = new-object psobject -property $properties
    $csv += $psobject
}
$command.EndExecuteReader()
$csv|export-csv c:\perflogs\export.csv

`sim_audit_get_searches_for_groups(*)`
      | stats min(_time) as _time, values(user) as user, max(total_run_time) as total_run_time, first(search) as search, first(search_type) as search_type, first(apiStartTime) as apiStartTime, first(apiEndTime) as apiEndTime by search_id, host
      | where isnotnull(search) AND search_type="ad hoc" | search user="*" search="*"
            | eval earliest = case(like(apiStartTime, "%ZERO_TIME%") AND like(apiEndTime, "%ZERO_TIME%"), "all time", like(apiStartTime, "%ZERO_TIME%"), "-", 1 == 1, apiStartTime )
            | eval latest = case(like(apiStartTime, "%ZERO_TIME%") AND like(apiEndTime, "%ZERO_TIME%"), "all time", like(apiEndTime, "%ZERO_TIME%"), "-", 1 == 1, apiEndTime )
            | `sim_time_format(_time)`
            | stats max(total_run_time) as total_run_time by search, _time, earliest, latest, search_type, user, host, search_id
            | sort - total_run_time
            | eval total_run_time = if(isnotnull(total_run_time), total_run_time, "-")
            | fields search, total_run_time, _time, earliest, latest, search_type, user, host, search_id
            | rename search as "Report Name/Search String", total_run_time as "Search Runtime", _time as "Search Start", earliest as "Earliest Time", latest as "Latest Time", search_type as Type, user as "User", host as "Host", search_id as SID
            | fieldformat "Search Runtime" = `sim_convert_runtime('Search Runtime')`

title: Zerologon Exploitation Indicators (CVE-2020-1472)
summary: Surfaces Netlogon secure-channel warnings and suspicious machine account password resets consistent with a Zerologon attack.
purpose: Zerologon (CVE-2020-1472) abuses a flaw in the Netlogon Remote Protocol to reset a domain controller's machine account password to an empty value, allowing an attacker to impersonate the DC. Windows logs a specific Netlogon warning when a client uses a vulnerable, unauthenticated secure channel connection; correlating that with an unexpected machine account password change on the same computer object is a strong Windows-native indicator worth investigating immediately.
spl:
(sourcetype="WinEventLog:Microsoft-Windows-Netlogon/Operational" EventCode=5829)
OR (sourcetype="WinEventLog:Security" EventCode=4742 TargetUserName="*$")
| eval signal=case(EventCode=5829,"netlogon_vulnerable_channel_allowed",EventCode=4742,"machine_account_password_changed")
| eval computer=coalesce(ComputerName, TargetUserName)
| stats count values(signal) AS signals earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY computer, Caller_Computer_Name
| where mvcount(signals)>0
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - last_seen

explanationSteps.description: Pulls Netlogon EventID 5829 (a vulnerable, unauthenticated secure channel connection was allowed) and Security EventID 4742 (a computer account was changed) restricted to machine accounts (names ending in $).
Labels each event with a human-readable signal name for the two indicators being correlated.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count values(signal) AS signals earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY computer, Caller_Computer_Name
explanationSteps.description: Groups both signal types by the affected computer object and the calling host, so a computer showing both a vulnerable-channel warning and a password change stands out.
Surfaces the most recent activity first for triage.

customisationNotes: Requires the Netlogon debug/operational log to be collected — enable and forward Microsoft-Windows-Netlogon/Operational in addition to the standard Security log.
Replace <windows_index> with your deployed Windows index.

A single EventID 5829 without a following 4742 machine-account password change is lower urgency but still worth reviewing — legitimate legacy devices can trigger 5829 on patched, mitigated domain controllers.
performanceNotes: Netlogon operational logs are typically low-volume compared to the Security log, so this search is inexpensive; still restrict the time range in production.
Consider tstats against an accelerated Authentication/Change data model if these sourcetypes are CIM-mapped in your environment.
prerequisites: Netlogon debug logging (Microsoft-Windows-Netlogon/Operational) forwarded to Splunk
Domain controller Security event log forwarded to Splunk

falsePositives: Legacy or misconfigured devices that legitimately fail Netlogon's stronger authentication can trigger EventID 5829 on a DC that has enforced mode enabled without impact.

Routine, scheduled machine account password rotation (default every 30 days) will show 4742 events unrelated to any attack — the correlation with 5829 in a short window is the key signal, not either event alone.
investigationSteps: Confirm whether the domain controller has Netlogon enforcement mode enabled (patched and configured per Microsoft's guidance for CVE-2020-1472).
Check whether the machine account's password was reset to empty or an unexpected value immediately after the 5829 event.
Identify the source host (Caller_Computer_Name) and investigate what process initiated the Netlogon connection.
drilldowns: Pull all authentication activity from the calling host in the surrounding 30 minutes.
Check whether the affected domain controller's machine account was used for any privileged operations shortly after the password change.

references.label: Microsoft Security Advisory
references.url: Microsoft: Netlogon Elevation of Privilege Vulnerability (CVE-2020-1472)

author: SPL Library Team

title: Possible Pass-the-Hash via NTLM Network Logon
summary: Flags NTLM network logons (Type 3) using elevated or service-style accounts, a common Pass-the-Hash pattern.
purpose: Pass-the-Hash (PtH) reuses a captured NTLM hash to authenticate without knowing the plaintext password, almost always appearing as an NTLM-authenticated network logon (Logon Type 3) rather than an interactive one. This search looks for NTLM network logons by accounts that are unlikely to legitimately authenticate that way — administrative or service accounts — as a starting point for investigation.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=3 Authentication_Package=NTLM
| eval user=coalesce(TargetUserName, user)
| eval src=coalesce(IpAddress, src)
| where NOT match(user, "(?i)\$$") AND (match(user, "(?i)admin") OR match(user, "(?i)svc") OR match(user, "(?i)service"))
| stats count min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime values(src) AS sourceAddresses values(ComputerName) AS targetHosts BY user
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves successful network logons (Type 3) authenticated via NTLM rather than Kerberos.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval user=coalesce(TargetUserName, user) | eval src=coalesce(IpAddress, src)
explanationSteps.description: Normalizes field names across slightly different Windows TA field extractions.

explanationSteps.spl: | where NOT match(user, "(?i)\$$") AND (match(user, "(?i)admin") OR match(user, "(?i)svc") OR match(user, "(?i)service"))
explanationSteps.description: Excludes machine accounts and narrows to account names that look administrative or service-related — adjust this pattern to match your naming convention.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime values(src) AS sourceAddresses values(ComputerName) AS targetHosts BY user
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes how often, from where, and to which hosts each matching account authenticated via NTLM.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index and adjust the account-name pattern to match your organization's admin/service account naming convention.
NTLM network logons are legitimate for many service accounts — baseline expected source hosts before treating a hit as high severity.
If Kerberos is fully enforced in your environment, any NTLM network logon by a privileged account is worth a closer look regardless of the naming pattern.
performanceNotes: This is a raw Security-log search; if the Authentication data model is accelerated in your environment, an equivalent tstats search restricted to Logon_Type=3 and Authentication_Package=NTLM will run significantly faster over long time ranges.

falsePositives: Legitimate service accounts that are configured to use NTLM (some legacy applications and appliances only support NTLM) will appear here routinely — baseline them.
Cross-domain or cross-forest authentication without a trust that supports Kerberos can force NTLM even for normal user activity.
investigationSteps: Check whether the source host is one this account is expected to authenticate from.

Determine whether a legitimate interactive session for the same account exists around the same time, or whether this is the only authentication activity — PtH rarely involves a prior interactive logon on the source host.
Review what the account did on the target host immediately after authenticating.
drilldowns: Pull all logon activity (all types) for this account across the full environment in the surrounding hour.
Search for process creation on the source host that could indicate a credential-dumping tool.

references.label: MITRE ATT&CK
references.url: MITRE ATT&CK T1550.002 — Use Alternate Authentication Material: Pass the Hash

author: SPL Library Team

title: Possible Passwords Typed Into the Username Field
summary: Finds failed logon attempts where the attempted username looks like a password, suggesting a user mistyped credentials into the wrong field.
purpose: Users occasionally type their password into the username field by mistake — for example on a screen-unlock prompt after a timeout. Because Windows logs the failed logon attempt including the invalid username, this can inadvertently leak a plaintext (or near-plaintext) password into the Security event log. This search flags failed logons whose target username looks unusually complex for a real account name, so the affected account's password can be rotated and the log entries handled per your data-handling policy.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4625
| eval user=TargetUserName
| eval looks_like_password=if(len(user)>=8 AND match(user,"[A-Z]") AND match(user,"[a-z]") AND match(user,"[0-9]") AND match(user,"[^A-Za-z0-9]"),1,0)
| where looks_like_password=1
| stats count min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime values(src) AS sourceAddresses BY ComputerName
| convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves failed logon events, which record the attempted (and rejected) username.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval looks_like_password=if(len(user)>=8 AND match(user,"[A-Z]") AND match(user,"[a-z]") AND match(user,"[0-9]") AND match(user,"[^A-Za-z0-9]"),1,0)
explanationSteps.description: Applies a simple complexity heuristic — length plus mixed case, digits, and a symbol — to flag usernames that look like they were actually a password.
Keeps only the events matching that heuristic.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count min(_time) AS firstTime max(_time) AS lastTime values(src) AS sourceAddresses BY ComputerName
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes affected hosts, since the specific leaked value itself should not be routinely displayed on a dashboard.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
This is a heuristic, not a guarantee — tune the complexity thresholds to your organization's real password policy to reduce false positives.

Handle any matching raw events carefully: they may contain a real, currently-valid password. Restrict access to the underlying raw search and rotate the affected account's credentials as a precaution.
Consider excluding this field from the table/output entirely in shared dashboards, showing only the host and count as done here.
performanceNotes: Low-volume, field-level regex match on already-filtered EventCode=4625 events — inexpensive at normal failed-logon rates.

falsePositives: Some organizations have genuinely complex service account names that can match the heuristic — review and adjust thresholds.
Automated systems retrying stale cached credentials after a password rotation can also produce complex-looking failed usernames.
investigationSteps: Identify the real account this likely belongs to (often the same user's valid account authenticates successfully shortly after from the same host).
Treat the exposed value as a compromised credential and force a password reset for the affected account.
Confirm log retention and access controls limit who can view the raw event containing the leaked value.
drilldowns: Review the account's authentication history for the following successful logon to confirm identity.

author: SPL Library Team

title: User Account Created and Deleted Within 24 Hours
summary: Correlates account creation (4720) and deletion (4726) events to flag accounts that existed for less than a day.
purpose: A user account that is created and deleted again within a very short window can indicate an attacker establishing and then covering up a foothold account, or a misconfigured provisioning/deprovisioning automation. This search pairs each account's creation and deletion events and flags short-lived accounts for review.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4720 OR EventCode=4726)
| eval action=if(EventCode=4720,"created","deleted")
| eval user=TargetUserName
| stats earliest(eval(if(action="created",_time,null()))) AS created_time latest(eval(if(action="deleted",_time,null()))) AS deleted_time values(action) AS actions BY user
| where isnotnull(created_time) AND isnotnull(deleted_time)
| eval lifespan_hours=round((deleted_time-created_time)/3600,2)
| where lifespan_hours<24
| convert ctime(created_time) ctime(deleted_time)
| sort lifespan_hours

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves account creation (4720) and account deletion (4726) events.
Labels each event and normalizes the username field.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats earliest(eval(if(action="created",_time,null()))) AS created_time latest(eval(if(action="deleted",_time,null()))) AS deleted_time values(action) AS actions BY user
explanationSteps.description: Pairs each account's creation and deletion timestamps by username.

explanationSteps.spl: | where isnotnull(created_time) AND isnotnull(deleted_time) | eval lifespan_hours=round((deleted_time-created_time)/3600,2) | where lifespan_hours<24
explanationSteps.description: Keeps only accounts where both events were captured in the search window and the lifespan was under 24 hours.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> and adjust the 24-hour threshold to match your organization's normal provisioning practices.

Requires both the creation and deletion event to fall inside the search's time range — widen earliest/latest if accounts might be created and deleted further apart, or run this daily against a longer lookback.
performanceNotes: The nested eval-inside-stats pattern is fine at normal account-management volumes; for very high-volume environments consider pre-filtering with a longer base search before the stats stage.

falsePositives: Legitimate short-lived contractor, test, or temporary accounts created by IT automation will also match — maintain an allowlist of expected temporary-account naming patterns.
investigationSteps: Identify who created and who deleted the account (Subject fields on the 4720/4726 events) — a mismatch is worth extra scrutiny.
Review what the account did during its short lifespan: group memberships granted, resources accessed, processes run.
drilldowns: Pull a full activity timeline for the account between its creation and deletion timestamps.

author: SPL Library Team

title: File Deletion Events from Windows Object Access Auditing
summary: Reports file deletion activity captured by Windows object access auditing (EventCode 4660/4663).
purpose: With object access auditing enabled on sensitive folders, Windows logs a handle-closed deletion event (4660) alongside the access-request event (4663) that shows the account, process, and object involved. This search surfaces deletion activity for investigation of data destruction, anti-forensic behaviour, or accidental deletion.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4663 Accesses="*DELETE*"
| eval user=coalesce(SubjectUserName, user)
| eval file=coalesce(ObjectName, object_file_path)
| stats count values(file) AS files_deleted BY user, ComputerName, ProcessName
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves object access events where the access mask includes a delete request.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval user=coalesce(SubjectUserName, user) | eval file=coalesce(ObjectName, object_file_path)
explanationSteps.description: Normalizes the acting user and target file path fields.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count values(file) AS files_deleted BY user, ComputerName, ProcessName
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes deletion activity by user, host, and the process that performed the deletion.

customisationNotes: Requires a SACL (System Access Control List) configured on the monitored folders and object access auditing enabled via Group Policy — this search returns nothing without that in place.
Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
Restrict the base search to specific paths of interest (e.g. finance shares, source code repositories) to keep volume manageable.
performanceNotes: Object access auditing can be extremely high-volume if enabled broadly — scope auditing (and this search) to specific sensitive directories rather than entire volumes.
prerequisites: Object access (SACL) auditing enabled on the monitored files/folders
Windows Security auditing policy configured to log object access

falsePositives: Routine file cleanup, temp-file deletion by applications, and normal user housekeeping will appear here — scope auditing to genuinely sensitive locations to reduce noise.
investigationSteps: Confirm whether the deletion was expected (e.g. part of a documented cleanup process) or unexpected.
Check whether the deleted files can be recovered from backup or shadow copies.
Review the acting account's other activity around the same time for signs of broader malicious behaviour.
drilldowns: Search for other object access events (read, write, rename) by the same user and process shortly before the deletion.

author: SPL Library Team

title: Successful Sensitive File Access via Object Access Auditing
summary: Reports successful read/write access to audited files and folders, for reviewing who accessed sensitive data.
purpose: When object access (SACL) auditing is enabled on sensitive files or shares, Windows records every successful access along with the requesting account and the specific rights granted. This search summarizes that activity so file access to a protected location can be reviewed for authorized use.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4663
| eval user=coalesce(SubjectUserName, user)
| eval file=coalesce(ObjectName, object_file_path)
| eval access_type=case(match(Accesses,"WriteData"),"write",match(Accesses,"ReadData"),"read",true(),"other")
| stats count BY user, file, access_type, ComputerName
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves object access attempts where auditing is enabled.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval user=coalesce(SubjectUserName, user) | eval file=coalesce(ObjectName, object_file_path)
explanationSteps.description: Normalizes the acting user and object path fields.
Classifies the access mask into a simplified read/write/other category.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count BY user, file, access_type, ComputerName
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes access counts by user, file, access type, and host.

customisationNotes: Requires object access (SACL) auditing enabled on the target files/folders; without it this search returns nothing.
Replace <windows_index> and scope the base search to specific paths to control volume.
performanceNotes: Object access auditing volume can be very high if enabled broadly — audit only the specific sensitive paths you need to monitor.
prerequisites: Object access (SACL) auditing enabled on the monitored files/folders

falsePositives: Any normal, authorized access to the audited files will appear here — this is a reporting/review search, not itself a high-fidelity alert.
investigationSteps: Confirm the accessing account had a legitimate business reason to open the file.
Check for unusual access volume or access outside normal working hours for the account.
drilldowns: Compare against a list of users authorized for the specific file share or folder.

author: SPL Library Team

title: Failed Authentication Against a Non-Existent Account
summary: Flags failed logons with sub-status code 0xC0000064 (username does not exist) — a common account-enumeration signal.
purpose: Windows differentiates a failed logon caused by a bad password from one caused by an account that simply does not exist (sub-status 0xC0000064). A pattern of these failures, especially from a single source trying many distinct usernames, is a strong indicator of account enumeration or a username-guessing brute-force attack.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4625 Status=0xC000006D Sub_Status=0xC0000064
| eval user=TargetUserName
| stats count dc(user) AS distinct_usernames_tried values(user) AS usernames_tried BY src
| where distinct_usernames_tried>5
| sort - distinct_usernames_tried

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves failed logons specifically flagged with the sub-status code meaning the target username does not exist.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count dc(user) AS distinct_usernames_tried values(user) AS usernames_tried BY src
explanationSteps.description: Counts, per source, how many distinct non-existent usernames were attempted.
Filters to sources trying more than five distinct invalid usernames — adjust to your environment's baseline.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
Adjust the distinct_usernames_tried threshold based on normal noise in your environment (typos, stale scripts) versus genuine enumeration.
performanceNotes: Inexpensive: filters on indexed EventCode/Status/Sub_Status fields before aggregation.

falsePositives: Misconfigured applications or scripts using stale/incorrect service account names can generate repeated 0xC0000064 failures without any malicious intent.
Password managers or SSO agents retrying old cached usernames after an account rename can also trigger this.
investigationSteps: Determine whether the source is internal or external — external sources hitting this pattern warrant immediate blocking consideration.
Check whether any of the attempted usernames later succeeded from the same or a related source.
drilldowns: Search for any successful logons from the same source address in the following 24 hours.

author: SPL Library Team

title: User Logon Activity Outside Business Days
summary: Reports successful Windows logons occurring on Saturday or Sunday, useful for spotting unexpected weekend account use.
purpose: Weekend authentication activity by accounts that normally only work weekdays can indicate compromised credentials being used outside a legitimate schedule, or can simply reflect on-call/overtime work. This search reports weekend logons by user for review against expected schedules.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=2 OR Logon_Type=10
| eval user=TargetUserName
| eval day_of_week=strftime(_time,"%A")
| where day_of_week="Saturday" OR day_of_week="Sunday"
| stats count values(day_of_week) AS days values(ComputerName) AS hosts earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY user
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - count

explanationSteps.spl: index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4624 Logon_Type=2 OR Logon_Type=10
explanationSteps.description: Retrieves successful interactive (Type 2) and remote interactive/RDP (Type 10) logons.
Derives the day of week from the event timestamp.
Keeps only weekend events.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count values(day_of_week) AS days values(ComputerName) AS hosts earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY user
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes weekend logon activity per user.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
This reports on the Splunk search head's configured timezone by default — set an explicit timezone conversion if your DCs and analysts span multiple timezones.
Cross-reference against a list of on-call or scheduled weekend-shift staff before treating results as anomalous.
performanceNotes: Inexpensive at typical logon volumes; restrict Logon_Type as needed to reduce noise from service/network logons that aren't meaningful for this report.

falsePositives: Legitimate on-call, overtime, or scheduled weekend maintenance work will regularly appear here — this is a review report, not a high-fidelity alert on its own.
investigationSteps: Check whether the user or their manager can confirm planned weekend work.
Review what the account did during the session for anything inconsistent with routine maintenance.
drilldowns: Pull the full session activity timeline for the flagged user during the weekend window.

author: SPL Library Team

title: Time Between Privileged Group Membership Granted and Revoked
summary: Pairs privileged group addition (4728/4732/4756) and removal (4729/4733/4757) events to measure how long an account held elevated access.
purpose: Temporary elevation to a privileged group (for example during a change window) should be time-bound. This search pairs each account's addition-to and removal-from a privileged group to measure how long elevated access was actually held, surfacing accounts that kept privileged membership far longer than expected — or that were never removed at all within the search window.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4728 OR EventCode=4729 OR EventCode=4732 OR EventCode=4733 OR EventCode=4756 OR EventCode=4757)
| eval action=if(EventCode IN (4728,4732,4756),"granted","revoked")
| eval user=MemberName
| eval group=TargetUserName
| stats earliest(eval(if(action="granted",_time,null()))) AS granted_time latest(eval(if(action="revoked",_time,null()))) AS revoked_time BY user, group
| eval held_hours=if(isnotnull(granted_time) AND isnotnull(revoked_time),round((revoked_time-granted_time)/3600,2),null())
| eval status=case(isnotnull(held_hours),"revoked",isnull(revoked_time) AND isnotnull(granted_time),"still elevated",true(),"unknown")
| convert ctime(granted_time) ctime(revoked_time)
| sort - held_hours

explanationSteps.spl: index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4728 OR EventCode=4729 OR EventCode=4732 OR EventCode=4733 OR EventCode=4756 OR EventCode=4757)
explanationSteps.description: Retrieves member-added and member-removed events for global, local, and universal security groups.
Labels each event as a grant or a revoke based on its event code.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats earliest(eval(if(action="granted",_time,null()))) AS granted_time latest(eval(if(action="revoked",_time,null()))) AS revoked_time BY user, group
explanationSteps.description: Pairs the earliest grant with the latest revoke for each user/group combination.
Calculates how long the membership was held, in hours, when both events are present.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> and confirm the group-management event codes match the group types (global/local/universal) used in your domain.
Widen the search's time range if grants and revokes for the same membership often fall further apart than a single day.
Rows with status="still elevated" and no revoked_time mean no removal event was found in the search window — investigate whether that access is still needed.
performanceNotes: Group management events are typically low volume; this search is inexpensive even over multi-week ranges.

falsePositives: Legitimate long-running privileged roles (e.g. a dedicated admin account) will show large held_hours values or no revoke at all — cross-reference against your access-review policy rather than treating every long duration as an incident.
investigationSteps: Confirm the elevation was tied to an approved change ticket or access request.
For accounts still elevated, confirm whether that access is still required.
drilldowns: Review what privileged actions the account performed while it held elevated membership.

title: Workstation Lock Duration by User and Host
summary: Pairs workstation lock (4800) and unlock (4801) events to report how long sessions stayed locked.
purpose: Windows logs when a session is locked and unlocked. Pairing those events gives a simple, privacy-respecting way to understand workstation idle/lock patterns per host — useful for physical security reviews, badge-vs-lock correlation, or spotting workstations that are never locked.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security (EventCode=4800 OR EventCode=4801)
| eval action=if(EventCode=4800,"locked","unlocked")
| eval user=TargetUserName
| transaction user, ComputerName startswith="action=locked" endswith="action=unlocked" maxspan=12h
| eval lock_minutes=round(duration/60,2)
| table _time user ComputerName lock_minutes eventcount
| sort - lock_minutes

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves workstation lock (4800) and unlock (4801) events.
Labels each event as a lock or unlock action.

explanationSteps.spl: | transaction user, ComputerName startswith="action=locked" endswith="action=unlocked" maxspan=12h
explanationSteps.description: Groups each lock event with its matching unlock event for the same user and host, capping the pairing window at 12 hours.
Converts the transaction's duration (in seconds) into minutes for readability.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
`transaction` does not scale well over very large time ranges — run this over a bounded window (a day or a shift) rather than months of history.
Sessions still locked at the end of the search window will not produce a paired row since no matching unlock event exists yet.
performanceNotes: Uses `transaction`, which is single-threaded and can be slow at scale — for a long-running dashboard, consider precomputing with `streamstats`/`stats` using earliest/latest per session instead.

investigationSteps: Compare unusually long lock durations against expected working patterns.
Cross-reference workstations that show no lock events at all against your lock-screen policy compliance.

author: SPL Library Team

title: Special Privilege Assignment at Logon (Token Elevation)
summary: Reports EventCode 4672 (special privileges assigned to new logon) for accounts and hosts, highlighting where sensitive privileges are being granted.
purpose: EventCode 4672 fires whenever a logon session is assigned one or more sensitive privileges (such as SeDebugPrivilege or SeTcbPrivilege), which typically only happens for administrative accounts. Reviewing this alongside the logon type and source helps confirm that privileged tokens are only being issued where expected, and can surface accounts that unexpectedly received elevated rights.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4672
| eval user=SubjectUserName
| where NOT match(user, "(?i)\$$") AND NOT match(user, "(?i)^(SYSTEM|LOCAL SERVICE|NETWORK SERVICE)$")
| stats count values(PrivilegeList) AS privileges_assigned earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY user, ComputerName
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves special-privilege-assignment events, which fire when a new logon session is granted sensitive privileges.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval user=SubjectUserName | where NOT match(user, "(?i)\$$") AND NOT match(user, "(?i)^(SYSTEM|LOCAL SERVICE|NETWORK SERVICE)$")
explanationSteps.description: Excludes machine accounts and built-in system identities, which trigger this event constantly and aren't useful for reviewing human/service account elevation.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count values(PrivilegeList) AS privileges_assigned earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY user, ComputerName
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes which privileges were assigned to which accounts, on which hosts.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
This event is extremely common for legitimate administrative and service accounts — baseline expected accounts and hosts before alerting on this alone.
Focus review on privileges like SeDebugPrivilege or SeTcbPrivilege appearing for accounts or hosts where they are not normally expected.
performanceNotes: EventCode 4672 can be high-volume on domain controllers and servers with frequent admin activity; keep the base search scoped to a bounded time range.

falsePositives: This event fires for virtually every legitimate administrative logon and many service accounts — it is only useful as a detection when scoped to unexpected accounts, hosts, or specific high-risk privileges, not as a blanket alert.
investigationSteps: Confirm the account and host combination is an expected source of administrative activity.
Review the specific privileges granted — SeDebugPrivilege and SeTcbPrivilege in particular warrant closer review outside known admin tooling.
drilldowns: Pull all logon and process-creation activity for the account on the same host around the same time.

title: Weekly Broken Events Report
summary: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. These events are been broken due to reaching the maximum number of lines limit. In the Monitoring Console, Indexing -> Inputs -> Data Quality has …
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. These events are been broken due to reaching the maximum number of lines limit. In the Monitoring Console, Indexing -> Inputs -> Data Quality has dashboards showing this information.
spl:
```The event that came in was greater than the maximum number of lines that were configured, therefore it was broken into multiple events... 
For a dashboard refer to the monitoring console Indexing -> Inputs -> Data Quality```
index=_internal AggregatorMiningProcessor "Breaking event because limit of" sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) `splunkadmins_weekly_brokenevents`
| rex "Breaking event because limit of (?P<curlimit>\d+)" 
| stats max(_time) AS mostRecent, min(_time) AS firstSeen, count by data_sourcetype, data_host, curlimit
| eval longerThan=curlimit-1
| eval invesLatest = if(mostRecent==firstSeen,mostRecent+1,mostRecent)
| rename data_sourcetype AS sourcetype, data_host AS host
| eval investigationQuery="```If no results are found prepend the earliest=/latest= with _index_ (eg _index_earliest=...) and expand the timeframe searched over, as the parsed timestamps from the data does not have to exactly match the time the warnings appeared...``` index=* host=" . host . " sourcetype=\"" . sourcetype . "\" linecount>" . longerThan . " earliest=" . firstSeen . " latest=" . invesLatest
| fields - firstSeen, longerThan, invesLatest
| eval mostRecent=strftime(mostRecent, "%+")
| sort - count

Also refer to the Monitoring Console, Indexing -> Inputs -> Data Quality
If you are in a (very) performance sensitive environment you might want to remove the rex/eval lines for the data_host field and let the admin update the investigation query manually```

| rex "Truncating line because limit of (?P<curlimit>\d+) bytes.*with a line length >= (?P<approxlinelength>\S+)" 
| rex field=data_host "(?P<data_host>[^\.]+)"
| eval data_host=data_host . "*"
| stats min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen, count, avg(approxlinelength) AS avgApproxLineLength, max(approxlinelength) AS maxApproxLineLength, values(data_host) AS hosts by data_sourcetype, curlimit
| rename data_sourcetype AS sourcetype
| eval hostList=if(mvcount(hosts)>1,mvjoin(hosts," OR host="),hosts)
| eval hostList="host=" . hostList
| eval avgApproxLineLength = round(avgApproxLineLength)
| eval invesLastSeen=if(firstSeen==lastSeen,lastSeen+1,lastSeen)
| eval firstSeen=firstSeen-10
| eval invesLastSeen=invesLastSeen+10
| eval investigationQuery="```Find examples where the truncation limit has been reached. The earliest/latest time is based on the warning messages in the Splunk logs, they may need customisation!``` index=* sourcetype=" . sourcetype . " " . hostList . " earliest=" . firstSeen . title: Valid Timestamp Invalid Parsed Time
summary: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. The timestamp was parsed but an error was thrown to advise that the timestamp does not appear to be correct.
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. The timestamp was parsed but an error was thrown to advise that the timestamp does not appear to be correct.
spl:
```The timestamp parsing did run but the timestamp found did not match previous events so the time parsing may need a review```
index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) (`indexerhosts`) OR (`heavyforwarderhosts`) 
"outside of the acceptable time window. If this timestamp is correct, consider adjusting" 
OR "is too far away from the previous event's time" 
OR "is suspiciously far away from the previous event's time" `splunkadmins_valid_timestamp_invalidparsed`
| rex "source::(?P<source>[^|]+)\|host::(?P<host>[^|]+)\|(?P<sourcetype>[^|]+)"
 ```The goal of this part of the search was to obtain the messages that are relating to this particular host/source/sourcetype, however since the message includes a time we cannot uses values(message) without getting a huge number of values, therefore we use cluster to obtain the unique values. Since we want the original start/end times we use labelonly=true```
| cluster labelonly=true 
| eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
| stats count, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen, first(message) AS message by host, source, sourcetype, cluster_label
```While "A possible timestamp match (...) is outside of the acceptable time window" and "Time parsed (...) is too far away from the previous event's time", result in the current indexing time been used, the "Accepted time (...) is suspiciously far away from the previous event's time" is accepted and therefore we need to expand the investigation query time to include this time range as well!``` 
| rex field=message "Accepted time \((?P<acceptedTime>[^\)]+)"
| eval acceptedTime=strptime(acceptedTime, "%a %b %d %H:%M:%S %Y")
| eval firstSeen=if(acceptedTime<firstSeen,acceptedTime,firstSeen)
```Now that we have the first message for each labelled cluster, we now take all relevant message per host/source/sourcetype```
| stats values(acceptedTime) AS acceptedTime, sum(count) AS count, min(firstSeen) AS firstSeen, max(lastSeen) AS lastSeen, values(message) AS message by host, source, sourcetype
| eval invesEnd=if(lastSeen=firstSeen,round(lastSeen+1),round(lastSeen)), invesStart=floor(firstSeen)
| eval invesDataSource = replace(source, "\\\\", "\\\\\\\\")
| eval investigationQuery="```Please note that this query may need to be narrowed down further before running it, this is an example only...``` index=* host=" . host . " sourcetype=\"" . sourcetype . "\" source=\"" . invesDataSource . "\" earliest=" . invesStart . " latest=" . invesEnd . " | eval indextime=strftime(_indextime, \"%+\")"
| eval firstSeen=strftime(firstSeen, "%+"), lastSeen=strftime(lastSeen, "%+")
| table host, source, sourcetype count, firstSeen, lastSeen, message, investigationQuery
| sort - count

title: Scheduled Searches That Cannot Run
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. As found in the Splunk monitoring console, moving it into an alert so we can get alerted to the problem rather than checking a dashboard/log about thi…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. As found in the Splunk monitoring console, moving it into an alert so we can get alerted to the problem rather than checking a dashboard/log about this. Can be fixed by the end user? Yes
spl:
```These searches are scheduled but for some reason cannot run (eg. invalid search syntax)```
index=_internal `searchheadhosts` sourcetype=scheduler NOT "The 'require' command received zero" `splunkadmins_scheduledsearches_cannot_run`
```Additional rex due to someone using app= inside their saved search name...```
| rex "app=\"(?P<app>[^\"]+)\""
| eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
| fillnull message
  ```The below 3 lines will catch map/lookup errors or similar that look like message="Error in 'map': Did not find value for required attribute 'attr'.". No actions executed. This may or may not be a good thing...``` 
| rex "- savedsearch_id=\"(?P<user2>[^;]+);(?P<app2>[^;]+);(?P<savedsearch_name_2>[^\"]+)" 
| eval savedsearch_name=coalesce(savedsearch_name,savedsearch_name_2), app=coalesce(app,app2), user=coalesce(user,user2) 
| fillnull status value="error" 
| eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster` 
| eventstats values(user) AS user by savedsearch_name, app, search_head_cluster 
| eval user=if(mvcount(user)>1,mvfilter(!(match(user, "nobody"))),user) 
| stats max(_time) AS mostRecentlySeen, values(success) AS success by message, savedsearch_name, app, log_level, user, status, search_head_cluster 
| stats count(eval(status="success")) AS successCount, count(eval(success==0)) AS reportFailureCount, count(eval(searchmatch("log_level=WARN OR log_level=ERROR OR status=delegated_remote_error"))) AS warnerrorcount, max(mostRecentlySeen) AS mostRecentlySeen, values(status) AS status, values(message) AS message by savedsearch_name, app, user, search_head_cluster
| where warnerrorcount>0
| append 
    [ search index=_internal `searchheadhosts` sourcetype=scheduler status=delegated_remote_error 
    | eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
    | eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster` 
    | stats max(_time) AS mostRecentlySeen, first(message) AS message by savedsearch_name, app, log_level, user, status, search_head_cluster] 
| selfjoin overwrite=true keepsingle=true savedsearch_name, app, user, search_head_cluster 
| append 
    [ search ```macro failures in the search syntax result in the log only appearing in splunkd, and the absence of delegated_remote_completion in scheduler.log``` 
        index=_internal `searchheadhosts` ERROR "failed job" sourcetype=splunkd `splunkadmins_splunkd_source` saved_search=* 
    | search ```Exclude time periods where shutdowns were occurring``` NOT 
        [ `splunkadmins_shutdown_time(searchheadhosts,0,0)`] 
    | rex "saved_search=([^;]+);(?P<app>[^;]+);(?P<savedsearch_name>.*?) err=" 
    | rex "(?P<messagewithoutheader>saved_search=.*uri=)http(s)?://[^/]+(?P<messagewithoutheader2>.*)" 
    | eval messagewithoutheader=messagewithoutheader . messagewithoutheader2 
    | eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
    | eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster` 
    | stats max(_time) AS mostRecentlySeen, first(message) AS message by messagewithoutheader, savedsearch_name, app, search_head_cluster 
    | eval log_level="ERROR" 
    | fields - messagewithoutheader 
    | sort - mostRecentlySeen] 
| selfjoin overwrite=true keepsingle=true savedsearch_name, app, search_head_cluster 
| where successCount<1 
| sort - warnerrorcount, savedsearch_name 
| rename message as Message, count as runCount 
| eval mostRecentlySeen = strftime(mostRecentlySeen, "%+") 
| fields - cluster_label, status, savedsearch_id, host, status

summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. These searches are either using index=* or not specifying an index at all and relying on the default set of indexes. Can be fixed by the end user? Yes…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. These searches are either using index=* or not specifying an index at all and relying on the default set of indexes. Can be fixed by the end user? Yes. Search Head specific? Yes. Uses the REST API.
spl:
| rest /servicesNS/-/-/saved/searches `splunkadmins_restmacro`
  ```Look over all scheduled searches and find those not specifying/narrowing down to an index, or using the index=* trick```
| table title, eai:acl.owner, description, eai:acl.app, qualifiedSearch, next_scheduled_time
| search next_scheduled_time!="" `splunkadmins_scheduledsearches_without_index` 
| regex qualifiedSearch!=".*index\s*(!?)=\s*([^*]|\*\S+)" 
| regex qualifiedSearch="^\s*search "
| regex qualifiedSearch!="^\s*search\s*\[\s*\|\s*inputlookup"
| rex field=qualifiedSearch "(?s)^(?P<exampleQueryToDetermineIndexes>[^\|]+)"
| regex exampleQueryToDetermineIndexes!="\`"
| eval exampleQueryToDetermineIndexes=exampleQueryToDetermineIndexes . "| stats values(index) AS index | format | fields search | eval search=replace(search,\"\\)\",\"\"), search=replace(search,\"\\(\",\"\"), search=if(search==\"NOT \",\"No indexes found\",search)"
| rename eai:acl.owner AS owner, eai:acl.app AS Application

title: Script failures in the last day
summary: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. Scripts or webhooks are throwing errors which may indicate an issue, requires "SearchHeadLevel - RMD5 to savedsearch_name lookupgen report" to tra…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. Scripts or webhooks are throwing errors which may indicate an issue, requires "SearchHeadLevel - RMD5 to savedsearch_name lookupgen report" to translate the search name accurately.
spl:
```Shell scripts running from Splunk are failing to run or throwing errors, or another sendmodalert failure has occurred``` 
index=_internal `searchheadhosts` sourcetype=splunkd log_level="ERROR" OR log_level="WARN" `splunkadmins_scriptfailures` command="runshellscript" OR ScriptRunner OR "Alert script returned error code" OR "ERROR sendmodalert" OR "WARN  sendmodalert" OR "Killing script" OR ("ERROR SearchScheduler" "sendalert") NOT sendemail.py NOT "InsecureRequestWarning" 
| bin _time span=30s 
| eval search_head=host
| eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster`
``` I'm unsure when the extra id appeared in here but it adds more context than threadid alone and reduces duplicates. Visible in 9.1.3``` 
| rex "^[^\[]+\[(?P<other_id>\S+)\s+(?P<threadid>[^\]]+)" 
| fillnull threadid other_id value="N/A" 
| stats values(_raw) AS _raw, values(search_head) AS search_head, values(search_head_cluster) AS search_head_cluster by _time, threadid, host, other_id 
| stats values(_raw) AS _raw, values(search_head) AS search_head, values(search_head_cluster) AS search_head_cluster by _time, threadid, host 
| search _raw!="*404: Not Found" _raw!="*Connection refused>" _raw!="*HTTP Error 403: Forbidden" _raw!="*Name or service not known>" NOT (_raw="*Connection reset by peer" _raw="*sendalert' command*") 
| rex field=_raw "[/\\\]dispatch[/\\\](?P<sid_from_dispatch>[^/]+)" 
| rex "sid:(?P<sid2>\S+)" 
| eval sid=coalesce(sid2,sid_from_dispatch) 
| eval sid=mvdedup(sid) 
| append 
    [ search index=_internal `searchheadhosts` sourcetype=scheduler WARN SavedSplunker maximum time allowed 
    | eval search_head=host 
    | eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster` 
    | stats count, last(event_message) AS event_message, last(component) AS component, latest(_time) AS _time, values(search_head) AS search_head, values(search_head_cluster) AS search_head_cluster by savedsearch_id 
    | rex field=savedsearch_id "^(?P<username3>[^;]+);(?P<app3>[^;]+);(?P<searchname>.*)" 
    | eval _raw = "count=" . count . " " . component . " " . event_message 
    | rex field=_raw "sid=\"(?P<sid>[^\"]+)" ] 
| `search_type_from_sid(sid)` 
| lookup splunkadmins_rmd5_to_savedsearchname RMDvalue AS report OUTPUT savedsearch_name
| eval searchname=coalesce(savedsearch_name, searchname) 
| `base64decode(base64appname)` 
| eval app4="N/A" 
| eval app=coalesce(app,base64appname,app3,app4) 
| eval _raw=mvindex(_raw,0,20), searchname=mvindex(searchname,0,20) 
| `base64decode(base64username)` 
| eval username=coalesce(username,base64username,username3) 
| fillnull value="N/A" app, searchname, username, search_head_cluster 
| stats count, values(_raw) AS _raw by app, searchname, username, search_head_cluster, _time 
| table _time, username, app, searchname, search_head_cluster, _raw

title: Users exceeding the disk quota
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. One or more users have reached the disk quota limit and may not be aware of this... Can be fixed by the end user? Yes. You may wish to use sendresults…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. One or more users have reached the disk quota limit and may not be aware of this... Can be fixed by the end user? Yes. You may wish to use sendresults with the output of this command...Search Head specific? Yes
spl:
```The listed users have reached the maximum disk quota, they may be unaware so it is best to let them know about this issue... 
Note that the REST API call accesses the jobs list which can expire for ad-hoc jobs in 10 minutes, so this may find zero results. The status.csv inside the dispatch directory records the size per job but it is not indexed by Splunk so either this alert needs to run very often or it will sometimes run after the issue has occurred and send an empty top 10 jobs list...
The introspection index version is called SearchHeadLevel - Users exceeding the disk quota introspection, it is not search head specific but it is also less accurate for disk space used```
index=_internal sourcetype=splunkd `splunkenterprisehosts` (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) "maximum disk usage quota" `splunkadmins_users_exceeding_diskquota`
| stats max(_time) AS mostRecent by username, reason, host
| eval mostRecent = strftime(mostRecent, "%+")
  ```We use this bizarre field naming so when we append the actual search results we don't have 20 columns of data to read, also it looks nicer in an email. However since we want this over multiple lines and we only want to run the map command once we use a temporary field which we later expand to a multi-line field. Furthermore mvexpand on the search field can result in multiple rows per search which is why a temporary field is used```
| eval renameToSearch="Why am I, " + username + ", receiving this? |" + reason + " (from) " + host + "|_|Last seen? |" + mostRecent + "|_|Your top 10 largest jobs are listed below"
| fields - reason, mostRecent, host
  ```The below is the complex attempt to include the largest jobs by querying the REST API. If we use map without the appendpipe we lose the original reason why we are sending this email. The initial workaround of makeresults and eval commands did work but this seemed slightly cleaner. Although there would be other ways to do this...```
| append [ | makeresults | eval username="workaround for map errors", body="to pass appinspect" ]
| appendpipe
    [
| map 
    [| rest /services/search/jobs `splunkadmins_restmacro` 
    | search ```Attempt to show the customer the top 10 jobs using disk and the related search commands/search names, also if it relates to their scheduled searches or not...``` author=$username$ diskUsage>0 
    | fields diskUsage, eai:acl.app, latestTime, label, provenance, runDuration, searchEarliestTime, searchLatestTime, title, updated, ttl 
    | rename title AS search, eai:acl.app AS app, label AS searchName 
    | sort - diskUsage 
    | eval diskUsage=round(diskUsage/1024/1024,2), searchEarliestTime=strftime(searchEarliestTime, "%+"), searchLatestTime=strftime(searchLatestTime, "%+") 
    | eval expiry=strftime(strptime(updated, "%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S.%3N%z")+ttl, "%+")
    | eval runDuration=substr(tostring(runDuration,"duration"),0,8) 
    | eval search=substr(search,0,300) 
    | fields - provenance, ttl, updated 
    | eval searchName=if(searchName=="","ad-hoc search",searchName)
    | eval renameToSearch="X"
    | table searchName, app, diskUsage, expiry, runDuration, searchEarliestTime, searchLatestTime, search, renameToSearch
    | head 10 ] 
]
| where username!="workaround for map errors"
| makemv delim="|" renameToSearch
| mvexpand renameToSearch
| eval search=if(renameToSearch!="X",renameToSearch,search)
| table username, searchName, app, diskUsage, expiry, runDuration, searchEarliestTime, searchLatestTime, search

title: Time format has changed multiple log types in one sourcetype
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. A changing time format is likely due to multiple log types using the same sourcetype or a date time parsing issue. A custom datetime.xml, ingest eval,…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. A changing time format is likely due to multiple log types using the same sourcetype or a date time parsing issue. A custom datetime.xml, ingest eval, or updating the source data may be required.
spl:
```This search detects when the time format has changed within the files 1 or more times, the time format per sourcetype should be consistent```
index=_internal DateParserVerbose "Accepted time format has changed" sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) (`indexerhosts`) OR (`heavyforwarderhosts`) `splunkadmins_timeformat_change`
| rex "source(?:=|::)(?<source>[^\|]+)\|host(?:=|::)(?<host>[^\|]+)\|(?<sourcetype>[^\|]+)"
| eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
| stats count, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS lastSeen by host, source, sourcetype, message
| eval invesMaxTime=if(firstSeen=lastSeen,lastSeen+1,lastSeen)
| eval invesDataSource = replace(source, "\\\\", "\\\\\\\\")
| eval potentialInvestigationQuery="```If no results are found, prepend the earliest=/latest= with _index_ (eg _index_earliest=...) and expand the timeframe searched over, as the parsed timestamps from the data does not have to exactly match the time the warnings appeared...``` sourcetype=\"" . sourcetype . "\" source=\"" . invesDataSource . "\" host=" . host . " earliest=" . firstSeen . " latest=" . invesMaxTime . " | eval start=substr(_raw, 0, 30) | cluster field=start"
| eval firstSeen=strftime(firstSeen, "%+"), lastSeen=strftime(lastSeen, "%+")
| fields - invesMaxTime, invesDataSource
| sort - count

title: Splunk Scheduler excessive delays in executing search
summary: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. Long latency delays in scheduled searches may indicate an issue, however the scheduled time of the search is what determine the search window. The…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. Long latency delays in scheduled searches may indicate an issue, however the scheduled time of the search is what determine the search window. Therefore this only shows when it has taken a long period of time to execute an actual search (there is another alert for skipped searches).
spl:
```These searches were scheduled to run at a particular time but the actual run time was more than X seconds later, which might indicate a search head performance issue 
In the environment this search was created on restarts are not overly common so we assume any restart might relate to a scheduling delay to prevent false alarms from the alert. This may need further tuning or you may wish to remove the where clause in this if you want more alerting.```
index=_internal `splunkenterprisehosts` sourcetype=scheduler app=* scheduled_time=* source=*scheduler.log
| search ```Exclude time periods where shutdowns were occurring``` NOT [`splunkadmins_shutdown_list(splunkenterprisehosts,600,600)`]
| eval time=strftime(_time,"%+") 
| eval delay_in_start = (dispatch_time - scheduled_time) 
| where delay_in_start>100
| rex "savedsearch_id=\"[^;]+;[^;]+;(?P<savedsearch_name>.*?)\"," 
| eval scheduled_time=strftime(scheduled_time,"%+") 
| eval dispatch_time=strftime(dispatch_time,"%+") 
| rename time AS endTime 
| table host,savedsearch_name,delay_in_start, scheduled_time, dispatch_time, endTime, run_time, status, user, app 
| sort -delay_in_start 
| dedup host,savedsearch_name,delay_in_start

title: Splunk Insufficient Permissions to Read Files
summary: Chance the alert requires action? Low. An insufficient permissions to read files error was thrown.
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Low. An insufficient permissions to read files error was thrown.
spl:
| tstats count groupby host, source
| append 
    [ search
        ```This search looks for insufficient permissions errors, the problem here is that we might have insufficient permissions to read a file but we might later obtain the correct permissions and then read the file (as permissions changes can happen *after* the file creation...this is why there is both a tstats listing all files (only done because I cannot find a nicer way to do this, map is possibly more compute intensive), and then a search for files```
        index=_internal "Insufficient permissions to read file" sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) OR (`splunkadmins_splunkuf_source`)
    | rex "\(hint: (?P<hint>[^\)]+)"
    | stats min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS mostRecent, values(hint) AS hint by file, host 
    | rex field=file "'(?P<source>[^']+)'" 
    | eval insufficientpermissions="true" 
    | fields firstSeen, mostRecent, source, host, insufficientpermissions, hint] 
| search ```Ignore any files requested by the macro, i.e. source!= or host!= or similar...``` `splunkadmins_permissions`
| stats sum(count) AS count, min(firstSeen) AS firstSeen, max(mostRecent) AS mostRecent, values(insufficientpermissions) AS insufficientpermissions, values(hint) AS hint by host, source 
| search ```If we have an insufficient permissions error, did we see no data from our tstats command?``` insufficientpermissions="true" NOT count=* `splunkadmins_insufficient_permissions`
    ```At this point if we see an insufficient permissions line, and we cannot see a result from the tstats showing indexed data from that file, then we have an issue, if not there is no issue with permisisons! 
    Insufficient permissions to read file + hint: No such file or directory when the file exists on a Splunk enterprise instance might require TAILING_SKIP_READ_CHECK = 1 in the splunk-launch.conf refer to splunk support for more info``` 
| eval invesSource=replace(source, "\\\\", "\\\\\\\\") 
| addinfo 
| eval investigationQuery="index=_internal \"Insufficient permissions to read file\" sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) OR (`splunkadmins_splunkuf_source`) earliest=" . info_min_time . " latest=" . info_max_time . " host=" . host . " file=\"'" . invesSource . "'\""
| eval firstSeen=strftime(firstSeen, "%+"), mostRecent=strftime(mostRecent, "%+") 
| fields host, source, firstSeen, mostRecent, hint, investigationQuery

purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Low. A potential indicator of poor index performance or an overloaded forwarder.
spl:

title: LDAP users have been disabled or left the company cleanup required
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. These users have been disabled or left the company but their users files are on the filesystem and this is therefore triggering warning or errors in t…
purpose:
Chance the alert requires action? High. These users have been disabled or left the company but their users files are on the filesystem and this is therefore triggering warning or errors in the Splunk logs, please cleanup the old user files for these users.
A separate alert should exist for orphaned searches...
spl:
```If we see a failed to get LDAP user 'username' from any configured servers then that is a sign the user is no longer in the company. However if there is also a message of Couldn't find matching groups for that same user it is more likely that they exist but just do not have access to Splunk
If you see this alert fire, than you probably need to cleanup the (for example) /opt/splunk/etc/users/... directory on each search head due to a user leaving/becoming disabled in LDAP. Alternatively they have a savedsearch/dashboard that you can find in the .meta files on the search head(s)```
index=_internal `searchheadhosts` "Failed to get LDAP user=\"" OR "Couldn't find matching groups for user=" OR (HTTPAuthManager "SSO failed - User does not exist") sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`)
| eval message=coalesce(message,event_message)
| dedup message 
| rex "SSO failed - User does not exist: (?P<user>\S+)"
| stats count, values(message) AS messages, values(component), AS components values(log_level), max(_time) AS lastSeen by user, host
  ```count=1 eliminates users who are failing to login...if a user is active in LDAP but fails to login we should not not get a "Couldn't find matching groups for user" line in the logs
If we are using a single sign on system and a user without any groups attempts sign on we should see the "SSO failed - User does not exist: <username> message"```
| where user!="undefined" AND user!="nobody" AND like(messages,"Failed to get LDAP user%") AND NOT like(messages,"SSO failed - User does not exist%")
| table user, messages, lastSeen, host
| eval lastSeen=strftime(lastSeen, "%+")

purpose: Chance the alert requires action? Low. A Splunk instance is advising that it cannot distribute to a peer node (indexer, another search head in the cluster or similar). Shutdown times are excluded.
spl:
```Unable to distribute to peer messages often indicate downtime or serious performance issues. The Unable to distribute to peer named status=Down scenario can also result from having many indexers and this may require an increase to the timeouts in distsearch.conf```
index=_internal "Unable to distribute to peer named" sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) `splunkenterprisehosts` `splunkadmins_unable_distribute_to_peer`
| rex "(?P<message>Unable to distribute to peer named (?P<peer>[^: ]+))"
| bin _time span=1m
| join type=outer peer
    [ rest /services/search/distributed/peers 
    | fields peerName, title
    | rex field=title "(?P<title>[^:]+)"
    | rename title AS peer ]
| eval targetHost=if(isnotnull(peerName),peerName,peer)
| search ```Exclude unable to distribute to peer messages where we sent the shutdown signal to the peer``` NOT [`splunkadmins_shutdown_list(splunkenterprisehosts,0,0)`]
| stats count, values(message) AS message, values(host) AS reportingHostList by _time, targetHost 
| eval reportingHostList=mvindex(reportingHostList,0,9)
| sort - _time
| where count>1

purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. Transparent huge pages should never be enabled on a Splunk enterprise server as per the https://help.splunk.com/en/?resourceId=Splunk_Installation_Systemrequirements. Uses the REST API.
spl:

summary: Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. This alert advises that a multi-line event is appearing in Splunk that is large enough that the default SHOULD_LINEMERGE = true setting may cause …
purpose:
Chance the alert requires action? Moderate. This alert advises that a multi-line event is appearing in Splunk that is large enough that the default SHOULD_LINEMERGE = true setting may cause blocking in the indexer aggregation queue, it's much more efficient to configure the SHOULD_LINEMERGE = false and LINE_BREAKER = ... if possible, note the TRUNCATE settings will likely need to be much larger to deal with the LINE_BREAKER change.

spl:
| tstats max(linecount) AS maxLineCount, min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS mostRecent, values(host) AS hosts, count AS occurrenceCount where index=*, linecount>250 groupby sourcetype
| search ```This search detects sourcetypes with greater than 250 lines which have SHOULD_LINEMERGE set to true, this might cause blocking in the indexer aggregation queue if there are a large number
of events with hundreds of lines or very large events such as >5000 lines of data. This alert is designed to give hints about where SHOULD_LINEMERGE=false / LINE_BREAKER=... might be more appropriate
Note that the REST API will return every instance of sourcetype, it's not quite as accurate a btool so this can generate false alarms if there are multiple props.conf definitions of a sourcetype```
`splunkadmins_multiline_linemerge`
| join [| rest `splunkindexerhostsvalue` /servicesNS/-/-/configs/conf-props
| fields title SHOULD_LINEMERGE
| search SHOULD_LINEMERGE = 1
| dedup title | rename title AS sourcetype]
| where maxLineCount > 260 AND occurrenceCount>30
| eval hostList=if(mvcount(hosts)>1,mvjoin(hosts," OR host="),hosts)
| eval hostList="host=" . hostList
| eval investigationQuery="index=* sourcetype=" . sourcetype . " " . hostList . " linecount>250 earliest=" . firstSeen . " latest=" . mostRecent
| sort - occurrenceCount, maxLineCount
| table sourcetype, maxLineCount, occurrenceCount, investigationQuery

spl:
```Detect search head issues related to extended search head downtime, in particular ConfReplication issues or KV store replication issues
KVStore - https://help.splunk.com/en/?resourceId=Splunk_Admin_ResyncKVstore , ConfReplication - https://help.splunk.com/en/?resourceId=Splunk_DistSearch_HowconfrepoworksinSHC (Replication_synchronization_issues)
The search head cluster captain is disconnected can relate to a SH cluster restart *or* if outside a rolling restart this may require a restart of the problematic search head...
In addition to this you could also look for "Error pushing configurations to captain" consecutiveErrors>1 , this would also hint at a potential issue although a small number of consecutive errors appears to be normal...
If you see the message "Consider performing a destructive configuration resync on this search head cluster member", then it's a real issue and often requires manual intervention...``` 
``` note that pull-based HF's often use kvstores for checkpointing and therefore this alert now works on those as well (not just search heads) ``` 
index=_internal `searchheadhosts` OR `heavyforwarderhosts` log_level IN (ERROR, WARN) "Local KV Store has replication issues" OR (component="ConfReplicationThread" "captain") OR (component="SHCMasterHTTPProxy" "Low Level http request" NOT "did not satisfy regex" NOT "does not exist" NOT "peer already has artifact" NOT "has inflight replications" NOT ("failed on report target request" "not found") NOT "unable to handle successful discard by peer" NOT "status is not UP") OR (component=SHCArtifactId "does not match") sourcetype=splunkd (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) NOT "Error creating snapshot" 
| eval search_head=host 
| eval search_head_cluster=`search_head_cluster` 
| search ```Exclude time periods where shutdowns were occurring``` NOT [`splunkadmins_shutdown_time(searchheadhosts,0,0)`]
| cluster showcount=true t=0.93 labelonly=t 
| stats min(_time) AS firstSeen, max(_time) AS mostRecent, values(_raw) AS _raw, max(cluster_count) AS cluster_count, max(consecutiveErrors) AS consecutiveErrors by host, cluster_label, search_head_cluster 
| eval firstSeen=strftime(firstSeen, "%+"), mostRecent=strftime(mostRecent, "%+") 
| where (match(_raw, "Error pushing configurations") AND consecutiveErrors>4) OR (match(_raw, "Error pulling configurations") AND consecutiveErrors>2) OR NOT match(_raw, "Error (pushing|pulling) configurations") OR (match(_raw, "Error (pushing|pulling) configurations") AND isnull(consecutiveErrors)) 
| eval _raw=mvindex(_raw,0,40) 
| fields - cluster_label, consecutiveErrors

purpose:
Chance the alert requires action? High. A duplicated licensing situation will normally require intervention to fix, this scenario can happen when a forwarder is not using the forwarder license or license master but is sending data into the indexers...
Another example can occur when the forwarder cannot connect to the remote license server, example log:
02-23-2024 02:24:03.876 +0000 WARN DistributedPeerManager [76946 DistributedPeerMonitorThread] - Duplicated License situation happen on peer=1531FB3B-6C49-46F8-BDA3-36B20ED7CD13 (losttext) because it has the same license key=B8632644E0D448E1BB9835BC6055FEEE33476A6A52AB5DEFBFDB3AB55A1983A7 as this searchhead=examplesearchhead but searchhead's license master=05FCEBDC-5184-3457-BECF-C0B4AFB538CA != peer's license_master=1531FB3B-6C49-46F8-BDA3-36B20ED7CD13 please fix this issue in 72 hours, otherwise search will be disabled.

```This warning will appear in the messages console of the license master, considering you have 72 hours to fix the issue you might want to be alerted about this so it can be fixed promptly! The scenario is likely to occur when a heavy forwarder is sending data into the indexers without using the forwarder license or talking to the cluster master.```
index=_internal `licensemasterhost` "Duplicated License situation happen" (`splunkadmins_splunkd_source`) 
| cluster showcount=true 
| fields _time, host, source, _raw, cluster_count

title: Detect MongoDB errors
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. If there are errors in the mongo (KV Store) log files on a search head cluster (unrelated to restarts) then this might indicate a kvstore issue which …
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. If there are errors in the mongo (KV Store) log files on a search head cluster (unrelated to restarts) then this might indicate a kvstore issue which needs attention.
spl:
```The main goal of this alert errors which might not appear in splunkd.log but are critical to keeping the kvstore running on the search heads. Please check the mongod.log file for further information, the additional count field is simply determining that mongo is still logging...
Attempt to find errors in the mongod log and make sure the errors do not relate to shutdown events in the search head cluster. Since this does will ignore any events when either cluster shutsdown it might not be sensitive enough for some use cases...```
index=_internal `searchheadhosts` `splunkadmins_mongo_source` (" E " OR " F " OR " W ") ```https://jira.mongodb.org/browse/SERVER-42078 advises this is harmless``` NOT "update of non-mod failed" NOT "is deprecated" NOT "No TransportLayer configured during NetworkInterface startup" NOT "interrupted at shutdown" `splunkadmins_mongodb_errors`
| regex _raw="^\s+?\S+\s+[EFW]" 
| search ```Exclude time periods where shutdowns were occurring``` NOT [`splunkadmins_shutdown_time(searchheadhosts,60,60)`]
| eventstats max(_time) AS mostRecent, min(_time) AS firstSeen by host
| bin _time span=10m 
| stats values(_raw) AS logMessages, max(mostRecent) AS mostRecent, min(firstSeen) AS firstSeen by _time, host 
  ```One final symptom that appears when mongodb is dead is the logging just stops, zero data, however this proved to be tricky in Splunk so the below query uses a few tricks to ensure the data will show zero values even if the server stops reporting. timechart was recommended by splunkanswers as it creates a timebucket with null values if no data is found...```
| append 
    [ | tstats prestats=t count where index=_internal `searchheadhosts` `splunkadmins_mongo_source` by host, _time span=5m 
    | search `searchheadhosts`
    | timechart limit=0 partial=f span=5m count by host 
    | fillnull 
    | untable _time, host, count 
    | stats max(_time) AS mostRecent, min(_time) AS firstSeen, last(count) AS lastCount by host 
    | where lastCount=0 
    | eval logMessages="Zero log entries found at this time, mongod might not be running, please investigate" 
    | fields - lastCount 
    | eval _time=now() ] 
| eval mostRecent = strftime(mostRecent, "%+"), firstSeen=strftime(firstSeen, "%+")
| fields _time, host, firstSeen, mostRecent, logMessages
| search ```Just in case...``` `splunkadmins_mongodb_errors2`

title: Cold data location approaching size limits
summary: Chance the alert requires action? High. One or more indexes are approaching the disk limits on their cold data, therefore the buckets will roll to frozen once this limit is reached. Only val…
purpose: Chance the alert requires action? High. One or more indexes are approaching the disk limits on their cold data, therefore the buckets will roll to frozen once this limit is reached. Only valid for non-SmartStore indexers. Uses the REST API.
spl:
| rest `splunkindexerhostsvalue` /services/data/indexes/ datatype=all 
    ```This search attempts to find indexes which are about to start rolling buckets to frozen due to disk space issues by checking how much percentage of the allocated cold section of disk is used. It does not take into account any volume sizing...
    This is the more proactive form of IndexerLevel - Buckets are been frozen due to index sizing``` 
| join title splunk_server type=outer 
    [| rest `splunkindexerhostsvalue` /services/data/indexes-extended/ datatype=all] 
| stats values(bucket_dirs.cold.bucket_size) AS currentColdSizeMB, values(bucket_dirs.home.warm_bucket_size) AS currentWarmSizeMB, max(bucket_dirs.home.event_max_time) AS latestTime, min(bucket_dirs.cold.event_min_time) AS earliestTime, min(bucket_dirs.home.event_min_time) AS earliestTimeHot, values(coldPath.maxDataSizeMB) AS coldPathSizeLimitMB, values(currentDBSizeMB) AS hotSizeMB, values(maxTotalDataSizeMB) AS maxTotalDataSizeMB, values(frozenTimePeriodInSecs) AS frozenTimePeriodInSecs, values(maxDataSize) AS maxDataSize, values(homePath.maxDataSizeMB) AS hotPathMaxDataSizeMB, values(bucket_dirs.home.warm_bucket_count) AS currentWarmCount, values(maxWarmDBCount) AS maxWarmDBCount by name, splunk_server 
| eval currentColdSizeMB=coalesce(currentColdSizeMB,currentWarmSizeMB), earliestTime=coalesce(earliestTime,earliestTimeHot)
| eval "Days of data based on epoch values"=round((latestTime-earliestTime)/3600/24) 
| rename name AS index, splunk_server AS indexer
  ```Things do get a little bit messy here, if the cold path size is unlimited, the remaining data is the maxTotalSizeMB minus what we have already used in the hot section (not a perfect calculation but close enough for our purposes``` 
| eval warm_bucket_percent = (100 / maxWarmDBCount) * currentWarmCount 
| eval coldPathSizeLimitMB=case(warm_bucket_percent>95 AND coldPathSizeLimitMB==0,maxTotalDataSizeMB-currentWarmSizeMB,coldPathSizeLimitMB==0 AND hotPathMaxDataSizeMB==0,maxTotalDataSizeMB,coldPathSizeLimitMB==0 AND hotPathMaxDataSizeMB!=0,maxTotalDataSizeMB-hotPathMaxDataSizeMB,1=1,coldPathSizeLimitMB) 
| eval percUsed=round((currentColdSizeMB/coldPathSizeLimitMB)*100,2) 
| eval frozenTimeInDays=frozenTimePeriodInSecs/60/60/24 
| eval maxDataSize=case(maxDataSize="auto","750",maxDataSize="auto_high_volume","10240",true(),maxDataSize)
| eval worstCaseBucketCountLeft=floor((coldPathSizeLimitMB-currentColdSizeMB)/maxDataSize)
| where percUsed>`splunkadmins_colddata_percused` 
| search `splunkadmins_colddata`
| table index, indexer, currentColdSizeMB, coldPathSizeLimitMB, percUsed, frozenTimeInDays, "Days of data based on epoch values", worstCaseBucketCountLeft
