summary: Report only? Yes. This report attempts to determine which lookups have not being used during a period of time, potentially allowing them to be deleted. This requires the summary reports "Ind…
purpose:
Report only? Yes. This report attempts to determine which lookups have not being used during a period of time, potentially allowing them to be deleted. This requires the summary reports "IndexerLevel - RemoteSearches - lookup usage", "SearchHeadLevel - audit.log - lookup usage", "SearchHeadLevel - Lookup Editor lookup updates" 
Additionally it relies on the lookup populated by "SearchHeadLevel - Lookup file owners". You may also wish to use "SearchHeadLevel - Lookups within dashboards", "SearchHeadLevel - Lookups within savedsearches" and "SearchHeadLevel - Lookup Watcher Recent Modification Summary" to not accidentally remove a lookup that will be used.
spl:
index=summary source IN ("IndexerLevel - RemoteSearches - lookup usage", "SearchHeadLevel - audit.log - lookup usage", "SearchHeadLevel - Lookup Editor lookup updates") ``` You may also wish to use the reports "SearchHeadLevel - Lookups within dashboards", "SearchHeadLevel - Lookups within savedsearches", just in case the lookup exists in a report/dashboard and "SearchHeadLevel - Lookup Watcher Recent Modification Summary" to check for updates``` 
| stats latest(_time) as lastUsedTime values(user) as user by lookup_file app search_head_cluster  
| join app, lookup_file type=outer 
    [| rest /servicesNS/-/-/data/transforms/lookups `splunkadmins_restmacro` search=type=file f=filename f=eai:acl* timeout=900 count=0 
    | rename eai:acl.app AS app, title AS lookup_file 
    | table app, lookup_file, filename, sharing ] 
| eval lookup_file=coalesce(filename, lookup_file) 
| append 
    [| inputlookup splunkadmins_lookupfile_owners 
    | rename "lastupdated" as "lastUsedTime"] 
| fillnull search_head_cluster value=`search_head_cluster`
| stats values(*) AS * by lookup_file app search_head_cluster
``` at this point we have the latest use by lookup_file but it's possible a lookup file definition name was used, not the lookup file name. So we lookup the lookup_file from the search and if it's matching a lookup_name we output the file name ```
| lookup splunkadmins_lookupfile_owners lookup_name AS lookup_file, app OUTPUT lookup_file AS lookup_file2
| lookup splunkadmins_lookupfile_owners lookup_name AS lookup_file OUTPUT lookup_file AS lookup_file_global
``` if the lookup file is globally shared we cannot use an app level match, only the lookup file name. However only the lookup names from searches will mention the lookup_file_gobal field and the definition only has a lookup_file ```
| eval lookups_combined=coalesce(lookup_file_global,lookup_file)
| eventstats values(sharing) AS sharing_global by lookups_combined, search_head_cluster
| eval lookup_file=if(sharing_global=="global" AND isnotnull(lookup_file_global),lookup_file_global,lookup_file)
| eval lookup_file=if(isnotnull(lookup_file2),lookup_file2,lookup_file)
``` now we can find the latest by the filename even if a lookup definition was used ```
| eventstats max(lastUsedTime) AS lastUsedTime by lookup_file, app, search_head_cluster
| eventstats max(lastUsedTime) AS lastUsedTime_Global, values(user) AS user_global by lookup_file search_head_cluster
``` if the lookup is globally shared the last used time in any app is counted as the last used time of the lookup ```
| eval lastUsedTime=if(sharing=="global",lastUsedTime_Global,lastUsedTime)
| eval user=if(sharing=="global",user_global,user) 
| eval lastUsedTime=strftime(lastUsedTime, "%+")
| stats values(*) AS * by lookup_file app search_head_cluster
``` if the owner is null the lookup doesn't exist (a potential false match by the summary searches) ```
| where isnotnull(owner)
| eval user=mvdedup(mvappend(mvappend(user,owner),owner_from_definition))

purpose: Report only? Yes. | rex "(?s), search='(?P<search>.*)\]$" 
| rex field=search mode=sed "s/\n/ /g" 
| rex field=search mode=sed "s/```.*?```/ /g" 
| eval search=if(substr(search,len(search),len(search)-1)=="'",substr(search,0,len(search)-1),search) 
| eval search_id=replace(search_id,"'","") 
| regex search="\|\s*loadjob\s*savedsearch=|\|\s*savedsearch|\|\s*map\s*(maxsearches\s*=\s*\S+\s*)?|\|\s*join\s+|\|\s*append(pipe|cols)?\s+|\|\s*set\s+|\|\s*union\s+" 
| rex field=search "\|\s*savedsearch\s+(\"(?P<identified_savedsearch_name>[^\"']+)\"|(?P<identified_savedsearch_name2>[^ '\)]+))" 
| rex field=search "\|\s*loadjob savedsearch=\"[^:]+:[^:]+:(?P<identified_savedsearch_name3>[^\"]+)" 
| rex field=search "\|\s*map\s*(maxsearches\s*=\s*\S+\s*)?(?P<identified_savedsearch_name4>(\"[^\"]+)|\S+)" 
| rex field=search "\|\s*join\s+[^\|]*?savedsearch:(?P<identified_savedsearch_name5>(\"[^\"]+)|\S+)" 
| rex field=search "\|\s*(append|appendpipe|appendcols)\s+\[.*?(?P<identified_savedsearch_name6>savedsearch\s+(\"[^\"]+|\S+))" 
| rex field=search max_match=50 "(?s)\|?\s*(union|set)[^\[]+(?P<part1>\[.*?\](\s*\[.*?\])+\s*(`[^`]+`\s*)*(\||$|',\s+))" 
| rex field=part1 max_match=50 "(?s).*?\[(?P<subsearch>.*?)\]\s*(\||$|)" 
| rex field=subsearch "(?s)^\s*\|?(?P<prepipe_subsearch>([^\|]+))" 
| nomv prepipe_subsearch 
| rex field=prepipe_subsearch max_match=50 "savedsearch\s+(?P<identified_savedsearch_name7>(\"[^\"]+|\S+))" 
| rex mode=sed field=identified_savedsearch_name4 "s/([\",']|savedsearch:)//g" 
| rex mode=sed field=identified_savedsearch_name5 "s/[\",']//g" 
| rex mode=sed field=identified_savedsearch_name6 "s/(\"|savedsearch )//g" 
| rex mode=sed field=identified_savedsearch_name7 "s/[\",']//g" 
| eval identified_savedsearch_name4=if(match(identified_savedsearch_name4,"(search=|\)|\[|\[\|)"),null(),identified_savedsearch_name4) 
| eval identified_savedsearch_name=coalesce(identified_savedsearch_name,identified_savedsearch_name2,identified_savedsearch_name3,identified_savedsearch_name4,identified_savedsearch_name5,identified_savedsearch_name6,identified_savedsearch_name7) 
```| table identified_savedsearch_name*, search, subsearch, prepipe_subsearch    ``` 
| where isnotnull(identified_savedsearch_name4) 
| search NOT identified_savedsearch_name IN ("instrumentation.topology*", "instrumentation.usage*", "instrumentation.upgrade*", "instrumentation.deployment*", "instrumentation.performance*", "instrumentation.app*", "instrumentation.licensing*", "instrumentation.authentication*") 
| eval method=if(isnull(identified_savedsearch_name3),"savedsearch","loadjob") 
| eval search_head=host 
| eval env=`search_head_cluster`

title: Suspicious File Download via Certutil.exe
summary: Detects certutil.exe used with download-capable flags (urlcache, verifyctl, URL) alongside an http(s) argument — a well-known LOLBin download technique.
purpose: certutil.exe is a signed Windows binary that can be abused to download remote files, bypassing some application allowlisting controls. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "Suspicious Download Via Certutil.EXE" (id 19b08b1c-861d-4e75-a1ef-ea0c1baf202b), which flags certutil invocations combining a download-capable flag with an http(s) URL.
spl:
index=<windows_index> (sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Sysmon EventCode=1 OR sourcetype=WinEventLog:Security EventCode=4688)
| eval Image=coalesce(Image, New_Process_Name)
| eval CommandLine=coalesce(CommandLine, Process_Command_Line)
| where (match(Image, "(?i)\\certutil\.exe$") OR match(OriginalFileName, "(?i)^CertUtil\.exe$"))
    AND (match(CommandLine, "(?i)urlcache ") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)verifyctl ") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)URL "))
    AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)http")
| table _time host user Image CommandLine ParentImage
| sort - _time

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves process creation events from either Sysmon or native Windows Security auditing, whichever this environment forwards.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval Image=coalesce(Image, New_Process_Name) | eval CommandLine=coalesce(CommandLine, Process_Command_Line)
explanationSteps.description: Normalizes field names between the two possible sourcetypes.

explanationSteps.spl: | where (match(Image, "(?i)\\certutil\.exe$") OR match(OriginalFileName, "(?i)^CertUtil\.exe$")) AND (match(CommandLine, "(?i)urlcache ") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)verifyctl ") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)URL ")) AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)http")
explanationSteps.description: Reproduces the Sigma rule's three conditions: the process is certutil.exe, the command line uses a download-capable flag, and it references an http(s) URL.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
Requires either Sysmon (EventCode 1) or native process-creation auditing (Security EventCode 4688 with command-line logging enabled) — command-line logging is not on by default.

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "Suspicious Download Via Certutil.EXE" (SigmaHQ, id 19b08b1c-861d-4e75-a1ef-ea0c1baf202b), authored by Florian Roth (Nextron Systems), Jonhnathan Ribeiro, oscd.community, and Nasreddine Bencherchali (Nextron Systems), licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
performanceNotes: Filtering on EventCode before the regex matches keeps this reasonably efficient; still restrict the time range in production.
prerequisites: Sysmon or Windows process-creation auditing with command-line logging enabled

falsePositives: Legitimate administrative use of certutil to retrieve certificates in constrained environments — baseline expected hosts/scripts that use this flag combination.
investigationSteps: Identify the parent process that launched certutil.
Determine what was downloaded and whether it executed.
drilldowns: Search for subsequent process creation from the downloaded file path.

references.label: Sigma rule: Suspicious Download Via Certutil.EXE (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id 19b08b1c-861d-4e75-a1ef-ea0c1baf202b — authors Florian Roth (Nextron Systems), Jonhnathan Ribeiro, oscd.community, Nasreddine Bencherchali (Nextron Systems); Detection Rule License 1.1

author: SPL Library Team (SPL logic derived from a public Sigma rule; see references)

title: Suspicious GrantedAccess Flags on LSASS (Credential Dumping)
summary: Flags process access to lsass.exe with GrantedAccess flags commonly associated with credential-dumping tools, excluding known-legitimate security products.
purpose: Tools that dump credentials from LSASS memory (a common precursor to Pass-the-Hash and lateral movement) request specific, unusually broad access rights when opening a handle to lsass.exe. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "Potentially Suspicious GrantedAccess Flags On LSASS" (id a18dd26b-6450-46de-8c91-9659150cf088), which flags a curated set of suspicious GrantedAccess hex values while excluding known-legitimate security tooling.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Sysmon EventCode=10 TargetImage="*\lsass.exe"
| where GrantedAccess IN ("0x1010", "0x1038", "0x1400", "0x1410", "0x1418", "0x1438", "0x143a", "0x1fffff", "0x1f0fff", "0x1f1fff", "0x1f2fff", "0x1f3fff")
| eval accessing_process=coalesce(SourceImage, Image)
| where NOT match(accessing_process, "(?i)\\(MsMpEng\.exe|MsSense\.exe|SenseIR\.exe|procexp\d*\.exe|procmon\d*\.exe|WerFault\.exe)$")
| stats count values(GrantedAccess) AS access_flags earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY accessing_process, host
| convert ctime(first_seen) ctime(last_seen)
| sort - count

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves Sysmon ProcessAccess events (EventCode 10) where the target of the access is lsass.exe.
Keeps only events where the requested access rights match a curated list of flag combinations commonly used by credential-dumping tools.

explanationSteps.spl: | eval accessing_process=coalesce(SourceImage, Image) | where NOT match(accessing_process, "(?i)\\(MsMpEng\.exe|MsSense\.exe|SenseIR\.exe|procexp\d*\.exe|procmon\d*\.exe|WerFault\.exe)$")
explanationSteps.description: Excludes well-known, legitimate processes (antivirus, EDR, Sysinternals, Windows Error Reporting) that routinely access LSASS with broad rights.

explanationSteps.spl: | stats count values(GrantedAccess) AS access_flags earliest(_time) AS first_seen latest(_time) AS last_seen BY accessing_process, host
explanationSteps.description: Summarizes remaining suspicious access events by the accessing process and host.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.
The excluded process list is a starting point — extend it with your own EDR/AV process names to avoid re-alerting on known-legitimate tooling in your environment.

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "Potentially Suspicious GrantedAccess Flags On LSASS" (SigmaHQ, id a18dd26b-6450-46de-8c91-9659150cf088), authored by Florian Roth, Roberto Rodriguez, Dimitrios Slamaris, Mark Russinovich, Thomas Patzke, Teymur Kheirkhabarov, Sherif Eldeeb, James Dickenson, Aleksey Potapov, and oscd.community, licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
performanceNotes: Sysmon EventCode 10 (ProcessAccess) can be high-volume — this rule already narrows to TargetImage=lsass.exe first, which keeps volume manageable on most endpoints.
prerequisites: Sysmon installed with a configuration that logs ProcessAccess (EventCode 10) events for lsass.exe

falsePositives: Security products and diagnostic tools not yet added to the exclusion list will trigger this — tune the exclusion list before relying on this as a high-fidelity alert.
investigationSteps: Confirm whether the accessing process is a recognized, authorized tool.
If unrecognized, isolate the host and treat as probable credential theft.
drilldowns: Search for follow-on lateral movement (NTLM network logons, new sessions) using credentials from the affected host.

references.label: Sigma rule: Potentially Suspicious GrantedAccess Flags On LSASS (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id a18dd26b-6450-46de-8c91-9659150cf088 — authors Florian Roth, Roberto Rodriguez, Dimitrios Slamaris, Mark Russinovich, Thomas Patzke, Teymur Kheirkhabarov, Sherif Eldeeb, James Dickenson, Aleksey Potapov, oscd.community; Detection Rule License 1.1

author: SPL Library Team (SPL logic derived from a public Sigma rule; see references)

title: AWS CloudTrail Logging Disabled, Updated, or Deleted
summary: Flags StopLogging, UpdateTrail, and DeleteTrail CloudTrail management events — a common defense-evasion step before other malicious activity.
purpose: Disabling or altering CloudTrail is a classic way for an attacker (or a misconfigured automation) to blind logging before further action. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "AWS CloudTrail Important Change" (id 4db60cc0-36fb-42b7-9b58-a5b53019fb74), which flags the StopLogging, UpdateTrail, and DeleteTrail management events.
spl:
index=<cloudtrail_index> sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail eventSource="cloudtrail.amazonaws.com"
| search eventName IN ("StopLogging", "UpdateTrail", "DeleteTrail")
| table _time eventName userIdentity.arn userIdentity.type sourceIPAddress requestParameters.name awsRegion
| sort - _time

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves CloudTrail management events specifically for the CloudTrail service itself.
Keeps only the three event names that indicate a trail was disabled, modified, or removed.

customisationNotes: Replace <cloudtrail_index> with your CloudTrail index.

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "AWS CloudTrail Important Change" (SigmaHQ, id 4db60cc0-36fb-42b7-9b58-a5b53019fb74), authored by vitaliy0x1, licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
Any hit on this search warrants immediate review — legitimate trail configuration changes are rare and usually performed by a small set of known automation roles.
performanceNotes: Inexpensive — filters on two indexed-ish fields before returning a small result set.
prerequisites: AWS CloudTrail configured to log management events, ingested into Splunk

falsePositives: Legitimate infrastructure-as-code changes to trail configuration (e.g. adding a new region) — maintain an allowlist of expected automation roles/users.
investigationSteps: Confirm whether the identity making the change is an expected administrator or automation role.
Check what other API activity occurred from the same identity/source IP immediately before and after.
drilldowns: Pull all CloudTrail activity from the same userIdentity.arn and sourceIPAddress in the surrounding hour.

references.label: Sigma rule: AWS CloudTrail Important Change (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id 4db60cc0-36fb-42b7-9b58-a5b53019fb74 — author vitaliy0x1; Detection Rule License 1.1

author: SPL Library Team (SPL logic derived from a public Sigma rule; see references)

title: AWS Root Account Usage
summary: Flags any non-service-event CloudTrail activity performed by the AWS account root user — root should almost never be used day to day.
purpose: AWS best practice is to avoid using the root account for routine operations. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "AWS Root Credentials" (id 8ad1600d-e9dc-4251-b0ee-a65268f29add), which flags CloudTrail events where the identity type is Root and the event was not an internal AWS service event.
spl:
index=<cloudtrail_index> sourcetype=aws:cloudtrail userIdentity.type=Root
| where eventType!="AwsServiceEvent"
| table _time eventName eventSource sourceIPAddress userAgent awsRegion userIdentity.accountId
| sort - _time

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves CloudTrail events where the acting identity is the account root user.
Excludes internal AWS service-generated events that are attributed to root but don't represent actual root user activity.

customisationNotes: Replace <cloudtrail_index> with your CloudTrail index.

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "AWS Root Credentials" (SigmaHQ, id 8ad1600d-e9dc-4251-b0ee-a65268f29add), authored by vitaliy0x1, licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
If root use is expected for a specific break-glass procedure, note the expected time window and requestor so hits outside that window stand out.
performanceNotes: Inexpensive — filters on the userIdentity.type field before returning results.
prerequisites: AWS CloudTrail configured to log management events, ingested into Splunk

falsePositives: Legitimate, rare break-glass root usage for account-level operations that can only be performed by root (e.g. closing an account) will also match — cross-reference against a change ticket or break-glass log.
investigationSteps: Confirm whether root usage was pre-approved.
Check the source IP and user agent against expected break-glass access patterns.
drilldowns: Pull all API activity from the same source IP address across the account in the surrounding period.

references.label: Sigma rule: AWS Root Credentials (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id 8ad1600d-e9dc-4251-b0ee-a65268f29add — author vitaliy0x1; Detection Rule License 1.1

author: SPL Library Team (SPL logic derived from a public Sigma rule; see references)

title: Registry Persistence via DbgManagedDebugger
summary: Detects a value written to the .NETFramework DbgManagedDebugger registry key outside the legitimate Visual Studio JIT debugger pattern — a known persistence trick.
purpose: The DbgManagedDebugger registry value normally points to the Visual Studio JIT debugger and is invoked automatically when a .NET application crashes. Pointing it at attacker-controlled code is a low-visibility persistence technique. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "Potential Registry Persistence Attempt Via DbgManagedDebugger" (id 9827ae57-3802-418f-994b-d5ecf5cd974b), which flags any value set on this key that doesn't match the standard Visual Studio debugger invocation.
spl:
index=<windows_index> sourcetype=XmlWinEventLog:Sysmon EventCode=13 TargetObject="*\Microsoft\.NETFramework\DbgManagedDebugger"
| where NOT match(Details, "(?i)^\"C:\\Windows\\system32\\vsjitdebugger\.exe\"")
| table _time host Image TargetObject Details
| sort - _time

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves Sysmon registry value-set events (EventCode 13) targeting the DbgManagedDebugger key.
Excludes the standard, legitimate value that points to the built-in Visual Studio JIT debugger, leaving only unexpected values.

customisationNotes: Replace <windows_index> with your Windows index.

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "Potential Registry Persistence Attempt Via DbgManagedDebugger" (SigmaHQ, id 9827ae57-3802-418f-994b-d5ecf5cd974b), authored by frack113, licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
performanceNotes: Very inexpensive — a specific TargetObject filter combined with a single exclusion regex.
prerequisites: Sysmon installed with registry event logging (EventCode 13) enabled

falsePositives: Non-standard but legitimate .NET debugging tooling configured by developers on workstations — verify with the owning team before treating as malicious.
investigationSteps: Identify what process set the registry value.
Determine whether the referenced executable exists and what it does.
drilldowns: Search for crashes of .NET applications on the same host following the registry change, which would trigger the hijacked debugger.

references.label: Sigma rule: Potential Registry Persistence Attempt Via DbgManagedDebugger (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id 9827ae57-3802-418f-994b-d5ecf5cd974b — author frack113; Detection Rule License 1.1

author: SPL Library Team (SPL logic derived from a public Sigma rule; see references)

title: Linux Download-and-Execute Pattern via Curl/Wget
summary: Detects curl or wget downloading into /tmp or /dev/shm combined with a shell execution invocation on the same command line — a common fileless-attack pattern.
purpose: A frequent Linux compromise pattern is downloading a script or binary into a world-writable temporary directory and immediately executing it via a shell, all on one command line. This search implements the detection logic of the public Sigma rule "Suspicious Download and Execute Pattern via Curl/Wget" (id a2d9e2f3-0f43-4c7a-bcd9-9acfc0d723aa), which requires all three of a downloader, a temp-directory path, and a shell invocation to appear together.
spl:
index=<linux_index> sourcetype=linux:audit type=EXECVE
| eval CommandLine=mvjoin(mvappend(a0,a1,a2,a3,a4,a5,a6,a7), " ")
| where (match(CommandLine, "(?i)/curl") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)/wget"))
    AND (match(CommandLine, "(?i)/tmp/") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)/dev/shm/"))
    AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)sh -c")
| table _time host CommandLine
| sort - _time

explanationSteps.description: Retrieves auditd EXECVE records, which log the full argument list of executed commands.
Reassembles the individual a0..a7 argument fields auditd logs separately back into a single command-line string.

explanationSteps.spl: | where (match(CommandLine, "(?i)/curl") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)/wget")) AND (match(CommandLine, "(?i)/tmp/") OR match(CommandLine, "(?i)/dev/shm/")) AND match(CommandLine, "(?i)sh -c")
explanationSteps.description: Requires all three indicators together: a downloader tool, a temp/shared-memory path, and a shell execution invocation.

customisationNotes: Replace <linux_index> with your Linux index; adjust the sourcetype if your environment uses a different auditd add-on's field naming (e.g. a pre-joined CommandLine field instead of a0..a7).

Detection logic adapted from the public Sigma rule "Suspicious Download and Execute Pattern via Curl/Wget" (SigmaHQ, id a2d9e2f3-0f43-4c7a-bcd9-9acfc0d723aa), authored by Aayush Gupta, licensed under the Detection Rule License (DRL) 1.1. This SPL is an independent implementation of that rule's logic, not a copy of its YAML.
performanceNotes: auditd EXECVE volume can be high on busy hosts — restrict the time range and consider pre-filtering on curl/wget in the base search if your sourcetype supports indexed field extraction on a0.
prerequisites: Linux auditd configured to log execve syscalls, ingested into Splunk

falsePositives: Legitimate deployment scripts and configuration management tools (Ansible, cloud-init) often follow this exact pattern — baseline expected automation and exclude known-good scripts by path or hash.
investigationSteps: Retrieve and inspect the downloaded file if still present.
Check outbound network connections from the host to the download source.
drilldowns: Search for process creation events spawned from the temp/shm path shortly after the download.

references.label: Sigma rule: Suspicious Download and Execute Pattern via Curl/Wget (SigmaHQ)
references.url: id a2d9e2f3-0f43-4c7a-bcd9-9acfc0d723aa — author Aayush Gupta; Detection Rule License 1.1

title: File Recovery From Backup Via Wbadmin.EXE
summary:
Detects the recovery of files from backups via "wbadmin.exe".
Attackers can restore sensitive files such as NTDS.DIT or Registry Hives from backups in order to potentially extract credential…
purpose:
Detects the recovery of files from backups via "wbadmin.exe".
Attackers can restore sensitive files such as NTDS.DIT or Registry Hives from backups in order to potentially extract credentials.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path="*\\wbadmin.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="WBADMIN.EXE" Processes.process="* recovery*" Processes.process="*recoveryTarget*" Processes.process="*itemtype:File*" by Processes.process Processes.dest Processes.process_current_directory Processes.process_path Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.original_file_name Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_path Processes.parent_process_guid Processes.parent_process_id Processes.process_guid Processes.process_id Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

purpose:
Detects tampering with autologger trace sessions which is a technique used by attackers to disable logging.
The AutoLogger event tracing session records events up that occur early in the operating system boot process.
Applications and device drivers can use the AutoLogger session to capture traces before the user logs in, and also used by security solutions as telemetry source.

title: Suspicious LNK Command-Line Padding with Whitespace Characters
summary: Detects exploitation of LNK file command-line length discrepancy, where attackers hide malicious commands beyond the 260-character UI limit while the actual command-line argument field suppo…
purpose:
Detects exploitation of LNK file command-line length discrepancy, where attackers hide malicious commands beyond the 260-character UI limit while the actual command-line argument field supports 4096 characters using whitespace padding (e.g., 0x20, 0x09-0x0D).
Adversaries insert non-printable whitespace characters (e.g., Line Feed \x0A, Carriage Return \x0D) to pad the visible section of the LNK file, pushing malicious commands past the UI-visible boundary.
The hidden payload, executed at runtime but invisible in Windows Explorer properties, enables stealthy execution and evasion—commonly used for social engineering attacks.
This rule flags suspicious use of such padding observed in real-world attacks.

title: Obfuscated PowerShell MSI Install via WindowsInstaller COM
summary:
Detects the execution of obfuscated PowerShell commands that attempt to install MSI packages via the Windows Installer COM object (`WindowsInstaller.Installer`).
The technique involves manip…
purpose:
Detects the execution of obfuscated PowerShell commands that attempt to install MSI packages via the Windows Installer COM object (`WindowsInstaller.Installer`).
The technique involves manipulating strings to hide functionality, such as constructing class names using string insertion (e.g., 'indowsInstaller.Installer'.Insert(0,'W')) and correcting
malformed URLs (e.g., converting 'htps://' to 'https://') at runtime. This behavior is commonly associated with malware loaders or droppers that aim to bypass static detection
by hiding intent in runtime-generated strings and using legitimate tools for code execution. The use of `InstallProduct` and COM object creation, particularly combined with
hidden window execution and suppressed UI, indicates an attempt to install software (likely malicious) without user interaction.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path IN ("*\\powershell_ise.exe", "*\\powershell.exe", "*\\pwsh.exe") OR Processes.original_file_name IN ("PowerShell_ISE.EXE", "PowerShell.EXE", "pwsh.dll") Processes.process="*-ComObject*" Processes.process="*InstallProduct(*" Processes.process="*.Insert(*" Processes.process="*UILevel*" by Processes.process Processes.dest Processes.process_current_directory Processes.process_path Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.original_file_name Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_path Processes.parent_process_guid Processes.parent_process_id Processes.process_guid Processes.process_id Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

purpose:

title: Potential Browser Data Stealing
summary:

purpose:
Adversaries may acquire credentials from web browsers by reading files specific to the target browser.

title: Registry Hive File Staged Outside Standard User Profile Path
summary:
Detects the creation of a registry hive file (UsrClass.dat or NTUSER.DAT) outside of the standard user profile path.
These files generally contain various user-specific registry settings and…
purpose:
Detects the creation of a registry hive file (UsrClass.dat or NTUSER.DAT) outside of the standard user profile path.
These files generally contain various user-specific registry settings and are typically located in the user's profile directory.
Staging these files outside of the standard path can be indicative of an attacker attempting to manipulate user registry settings
for persistence, privilege escalation, or dump user registry hives for credential harvesting.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem where Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\UsrClass.dat", "*\\NTUSER.DAT") NOT (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\Windows\\UsrClass.dat" OR file_pathCondition="true" OR Filesystem.file_path IN ("C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\*", "C:\\Windows\\SYSVOL\\*", "C:\\Windows\\ServiceProfiles\\*")) by Filesystem.dest Filesystem.file_create_time Filesystem.process_path Filesystem.process_guid Filesystem.process_id Filesystem.file_path | rex field=Filesystem.file_path "(?<file_pathMatch>(?i)^C:\\\\Users\\\\[^\\\\]+\\\\NTUSER\\.DAT$)" | eval file_pathCondition=if(isnotnull(file_pathMatch), "true", "false") | search Filesystem.file_path IN ("*\\UsrClass.dat", "*\\NTUSER.DAT") NOT (Filesystem.file_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\Windows\\UsrClass.dat" OR file_pathCondition="true" OR Filesystem.file_path IN ("C:\\Windows\\System32\\config\\*", "C:\\Windows\\SYSVOL\\*", "C:\\Windows\\ServiceProfiles\\*")) | `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

summary:

purpose:
Detects when an attacker modifies values of the Disk Cleanup Handler in the registry to achieve persistence via autorun.
The disk cleanup manager is part of the operating system.
It displays the dialog box […] The user has the option of enabling or disabling individual handlers by selecting or clearing their check box in the disk cleanup manager's UI.
Although Windows comes with a number of disk cleanup handlers, they aren't designed to handle files produced by other applications.
Instead, the disk cleanup manager is designed to be flexible and extensible by enabling any developer to implement and register their own disk cleanup handler.
Any developer can extend the available disk cleanup services by implementing and registering a disk cleanup handler.

purpose:
Detects potential abuse of WerFaultSecure.exe to dump Protected Process Light (PPL) processes like LSASS or to freeze security solutions (EDR/antivirus).
This technique is used by tools such as EDR-Freeze and WSASS to bypass PPL protections and access sensitive information or disable security software.
Distinct command line patterns help identify the specific tool:
- WSASS usage typically shows: "WSASS.exe WerFaultSecure.exe [PID]" in ParentCommandLine
- EDR-Freeze usage typically shows: "EDR-Freeze_[version].exe [PID] [timeout]" in ParentCommandLine
Legitimate debugging operations using WerFaultSecure are rare in production environments and should be investigated.

purpose:

title: NTLM Hash Leak Via Curl NTLM Authentication
summary:
Detects the use of curl with NTLM authentication and empty credentials (-u :), which can be abused to leak the currently logged-in user's NTLMv2 challenge-response to an
attacker-controlled …
purpose:
Detects the use of curl with NTLM authentication and empty credentials (-u :), which can be abused to leak the currently logged-in user's NTLMv2 challenge-response to an
attacker-controlled server, enabling offline cracking or relay attacks.
When no credentials are provided, the Microsoft-shipped curl passes a NULL identity to Windows SSPI, which automatically falls back to the current user's logon session credentials
stored in LSASS — without requiring a plaintext password.
This behavior is exclusive to the curl binary shipped by Microsoft (available since Windows 10 / Windows Server 2019), which is built with SSPI support.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path="*\\curl.exe" OR Processes.original_file_name="curl.exe" Processes.process="*--ntlm*" by Processes.process Processes.dest Processes.process_current_directory Processes.process_path Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.original_file_name Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_path Processes.parent_process_guid Processes.parent_process_id Processes.process_guid Processes.process_id Processes.user | regex Processes.process="(?i)\\s(-u|--user)\\s*:" | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

Validate field names and index/sourcetype placeholders against your own CIM mapping or Sysmon/Windows TA configuration before relying on this in production.

summary:

purpose:
Detects execution of the "finger.exe" utility.
Finger.EXE or "TCPIP Finger Command" is an old utility that is still present on modern Windows installation. It Displays information about users on a specified remote computer (typically a UNIX computer) that is running the finger service or daemon.
Due to the old nature of this utility and the rareness of machines having the finger service. Any execution of "finger.exe" can be considered "suspicious" and worth investigating.

title: Uncommon Link.EXE Parent Process
summary:
Detects an uncommon parent process of "LINK.EXE".
Link.EXE in Microsoft incremental linker. Its a utility usually bundled with Visual Studio installation.
Multiple utilities often found in t…
purpose:
Detects an uncommon parent process of "LINK.EXE".
Link.EXE in Microsoft incremental linker. Its a utility usually bundled with Visual Studio installation.
Multiple utilities often found in the same folder (editbin.exe, dumpbin.exe, lib.exe, etc) have a hardcode call to the "LINK.EXE" binary without checking its validity.
This would allow an attacker to sideload any binary with the name "link.exe" if one of the aforementioned tools get executed from a different location.
By filtering the known locations of such utilities we can spot uncommon parent process of LINK.EXE that might be suspicious or malicious.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_path="*\\link.exe" Processes.process="*LINK /*" NOT (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("C:\\Program Files\\Microsoft Visual Studio\\*", "C:\\Program Files (x86)\\Microsoft Visual Studio\\*") Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*\\VC\\bin\\*", "*\\VC\\Tools\\*")) by Processes.process Processes.dest Processes.process_current_directory Processes.process_path Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.original_file_name Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_path Processes.parent_process_guid Processes.parent_process_id Processes.process_guid Processes.process_id Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

title: Bad Opsec Defaults Sacrificial Processes With Improper Arguments
summary:
Detects attackers using tooling with bad opsec defaults.
E.g. spawning a sacrificial process to inject a capability into the process without taking into account how the process is normally r…
purpose:
Detects attackers using tooling with bad opsec defaults.
E.g. spawning a sacrificial process to inject a capability into the process without taking into account how the process is normally run.
One trivial example of this is using rundll32.exe without arguments as a sacrificial process (default in CS, now highlighted by c2lint), running WerFault without arguments (Kraken - credit am0nsec), and other examples.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_path="*\\WerFault.exe" Processes.process="*WerFault.exe") OR (Processes.process_path="*\\rundll32.exe" Processes.process="*rundll32.exe") OR (Processes.process_path="*\\regsvcs.exe" Processes.process="*regsvcs.exe") OR (Processes.process_path="*\\regasm.exe" Processes.process="*regasm.exe") OR (Processes.process_path="*\\regsvr32.exe" Processes.process="*regsvr32.exe") NOT ((Processes.parent_process_path="*\\AppData\\Local\\Microsoft\\EdgeUpdate\\Install\\{*" Processes.process_path="*\\rundll32.exe" Processes.process="*rundll32.exe") OR (Processes.parent_process_path IN ("*\\AppData\\Local\\BraveSoftware\\Brave-Browser\\Application\\*", "*\\AppData\\Local\\Google\\Chrome\\Application\\*") Processes.parent_process_path="*\\Installer\\setup.exe" Processes.parent_process="*--uninstall *" Processes.process_path="*\\rundll32.exe" Processes.process="*rundll32.exe")) by Processes.process Processes.dest Processes.process_current_directory Processes.process_path Processes.process_integrity_level Processes.original_file_name Processes.parent_process Processes.parent_process_path Processes.parent_process_guid Processes.parent_process_id Processes.process_guid Processes.process_id Processes.user | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

purpose: Detects the dual use tool ADExplorer writing a complete AD snapshot into a .dat file. This can be used by attackers to extract data for Bloodhound, usernames for password spraying or use the meta data for social engineering. purpose:

title: Directory Service Restore Mode(DSRM) Registry Value Tampering
summary:
Detects changes to "DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" registry value.
During a Domain Controller (DC) promotion, administrators create a Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) local administrator acco…
purpose:
Detects changes to "DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" registry value.
During a Domain Controller (DC) promotion, administrators create a Directory Services Restore Mode (DSRM) local administrator account with a password that rarely changes. The DSRM account is an “Administrator” account that logs in with the DSRM mode when the server is booting up to restore AD backups or recover the server from a failure.
Attackers could abuse DSRM account to maintain their persistence and access to the organization's Active Directory.
If the "DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" value is set to "0", the administrator account can only be used if the DC starts in DSRM.
If the "DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" value is set to "1", the administrator account can only be used if the local AD DS service is stopped.
If the "DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" value is set to "2", the administrator account can always be used.
spl: | tstats summariesonly=false allow_old_summaries=true fillnull_value="null" count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Registry where Registry.registry_key_name="*\\Control\\Lsa\\DsrmAdminLogonBehavior" NOT Registry.registry_value_data="DWORD (0x00000000)" by Registry.dest Registry.registry_value_data Registry.action Registry.process_path Registry.process_guid Registry.process_id Registry.registry_key_name | `drop_dm_object_name(Registry)` | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(firstTime) | convert timeformat="%Y-%m-%dT%H:%M:%S" ctime(lastTime)

purpose:
Detects potential credential harvesting attempts through LSASS memory dumps using ProcDump.
This rule identifies suspicious command-line patterns that combine memory dump flags (-ma, -mm, -mp) with LSASS-related process markers.

purpose:

NetExec is a PyInstaller-bundled binary that extracts its embedded data files to a "_MEI<random>" directory

Detects the creation of a dMSASvc account using the New-ADServiceAccount cmdlet in certain OUs.

summary:

purpose:
Detects usage of Windows Input Method Editor (IME) keyboard layout feature, which allows an attacker to load a DLL into the process after sending the WM_INPUTLANGCHANGEREQUEST message.

title: RDP Sensitive Settings Changed
summary:
Detects tampering of RDP Terminal Service/Server sensitive settings.
Such as allowing unauthorized users access to a system via the 'fAllowUnsolicited' or enabling RDP via 'fDenyTSConnection…
purpose:
Detects tampering of RDP Terminal Service/Server sensitive settings.
Such as allowing unauthorized users access to a system via the 'fAllowUnsolicited' or enabling RDP via 'fDenyTSConnections', etc.

Below is a list of registry keys/values that are monitored by this rule:

- Shadow: Used to enable Remote Desktop shadowing, which allows an administrator to view or control a user's session.
- DisableRemoteDesktopAntiAlias: Disables anti-aliasing for remote desktop sessions.
- DisableSecuritySettings: Disables certain security settings for Remote Desktop connections.
- fAllowUnsolicited: Allows unsolicited remote assistance offers.
- fAllowUnsolicitedFullControl: Allows unsolicited remote assistance offers with full control.
- InitialProgram: Specifies a program to run automatically when a user logs on to a remote computer.
- ServiceDll: Used in RDP hijacking techniques to specify a custom DLL to be loaded by the Terminal Services service.
- SecurityLayer: Specifies the security layer used for RDP connections.

purpose:
Detects the usage of wmic.exe to modify Windows registry via the WMI StdRegProv class write methods (CreateKey, DeleteKey, SetStringValue, etc.).

purpose:
Detects potential persistence behavior using the windows telemetry registry key.
Windows telemetry makes use of the binary CompatTelRunner.exe to run a variety of commands and perform the actual telemetry collections.

title: Attempts of Kerberos Coercion Via DNS SPN Spoofing
summary:
Detects the presence of "UWhRC....AAYBAAAA" pattern in command line.
The pattern "1UWhRCAAAAA..BAAAA" is a base64-encoded signature that corresponds to a marshaled CREDENTIAL_TARGET_INFORMAT…
purpose:
Detects the presence of "UWhRC....AAYBAAAA" pattern in command line.
The pattern "1UWhRCAAAAA..BAAAA" is a base64-encoded signature that corresponds to a marshaled CREDENTIAL_TARGET_INFORMATION structure.
Attackers can use this technique to coerce authentication from victim systems to attacker-controlled hosts.
It is one of the strong indicators of a Kerberos coercion attack, where adversaries manipulate DNS records
to spoof Service Principal Names (SPNs) and redirect authentication requests like in CVE-2025-33073.
If you see this pattern in the command line, it is likely an attempt to add spoofed Service Principal Names (SPNs) to DNS records,
or checking for the presence of such records through the `nslookup` command.

summary: Detects execution and usage of the DSInternals PowerShell module. Which can be used to perform what might be considered as suspicious activity such as dumping DPAPI backup keys or manipulati…
purpose:
Detects execution and usage of the DSInternals PowerShell module. Which can be used to perform what might be considered as suspicious activity such as dumping DPAPI backup keys or manipulating NTDS.DIT files.
The DSInternals PowerShell Module exposes several internal features of Active Directory and Azure Active Directory. These include FIDO2 and NGC key auditing, offline ntds.dit file manipulation, password auditing, DC recovery from IFM backups and password hash calculation.

title: Potential Persistence Via Disk Cleanup Handler - Registry
summary:
Detects when an attacker modifies values of the Disk Cleanup Handler in the registry to achieve persistence.
The disk cleanup manager is part of the operating system. It displays the dialog …
purpose:
Detects when an attacker modifies values of the Disk Cleanup Handler in the registry to achieve persistence.
The disk cleanup manager is part of the operating system. It displays the dialog box […]
The user has the option of enabling or disabling individual handlers by selecting or clearing their check box in the disk cleanup manager's UI.
Although Windows comes with a number of disk cleanup handlers, they aren't designed to handle files produced by other applications.

purpose:
Detects attempts to add, modify, or delete Windows Credential Guard related registry keys or values via command line tools such as Reg.exe or PowerShell.
Credential Guard uses virtualization-based security to isolate secrets so that only privileged system software can access them.
Adversaries may disable Credential Guard to gain access to sensitive credentials stored in the system, such as NTLM hashes and Kerberos tickets, which can be used for lateral movement and privilege escalation.
The rule matches suspicious command lines that target DeviceGuard or LSA registry paths and manipulate keys like EnableVirtualizationBasedSecurity, RequirePlatformSecurityFeatures, or LsaCfgFlags.
Such activity may indicate an attempt to disable or tamper with Credential Guard, potentially exposing sensitive credentials for misuse.

The "PromptOnSecureDesktop" setting specifically dete…
purpose:
Detects when an attacker tries to change User Account Control (UAC) elevation request destination via the "PromptOnSecureDesktop" value.
The "PromptOnSecureDesktop" setting specifically determines whether UAC prompts are displayed on the secure desktop. The secure desktop is a separate desktop environment that's isolated from other processes running on the system. It's designed to prevent malicious software from intercepting or tampering with UAC prompts.
When "PromptOnSecureDesktop" is set to 0, UAC prompts are displayed on the user's current desktop instead of the secure desktop. This reduces the level of security because it potentially exposes the prompts to manipulation by malicious software.

purpose:
Detects the execution of a script event consumer. When scrcons.exe launches, it does so in response to the creation of an ActiveScriptEventConsumer instance
and will execute registered JScript or VBScript code as a result.
Script event consumers are a built-in Windows Management Instrumentation (WMI) class that
automatically executes a predefined script (in VBScript or JScript) whenever a specific system event occurs.
Adversaries often abuse script event consumers to maintain persistence on a compromised host
by executing a malicious script whenever a specific event occurs.

purpose:

purpose:

title: Windows Vulnerable Driver Blocklist Disabled
summary:

purpose:
Detects when the Windows Vulnerable Driver Blocklist is set to disabled. This setting is crucial for preventing the loading of known vulnerable drivers,
and its modification may indicate an attempt to bypass security controls. It is often targeted by threat actors to facilitate the installation of malicious or vulnerable drivers,
particularly in scenarios involving Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) bypass techniques.
This rule applies to systems that support the Vulnerable Driver Blocklist feature, including Windows 10 version 1903 and later, and Windows Server 2022 and later.
Note that this change will require a reboot to take effect, and this rule only detects the registry modification action.

purpose:
Detects the execution of 'sudo' command with '--chroot' option, which is used to change the root directory for command execution.
Attackers may use this technique to evade detection and execute commands in a modified environment.

purpose:
